Need physical relation phases tied, but for incommensurate average independent okay.\n    ph_o=rng.uniform(0,2*np.pi,npoints)\n    ph_s=rng.uniform(0,2*np.pi,npoints)\n    # Rotating basis e1(t),e2(t) around s in inertial? Planet spin relative inertial, while spin axis fixed in inertial for this toy.\n    # material offset = q1*(cos ws t e1 + sin ws t e2) + q2*(-sin ws t e1+cos ws t e2)+q3 e3\n    # can combine transverse components A,B.\n    q1,q2,q3=q[:,0],q[:,1],q[:,2]\n    cs=np.cos(ph_s); ss=np.sin(ph_s)\n    # transverse position coeffs in e1,e2\n    A = q1*cs - q2*ss\n    B = q1*ss + q2*cs\n    # derivatives of offset:\n    # r' = w[-B e1 + A e2]\n    # r'' = -w^2[A e1+B e2]\n    # r''' = w^3[B e1 - A e2]\n    # r''''= w^4[A e1+B e2]\n    r1 = w*((-B)[:,None]*e1 + A[:,None]*e2)\n    r2 = -w*w*(A[:,None]*e1 + B[:,None]*e2)\n    r3 = w**3*(B[:,None]*e1 - A[:,None]*e2)\n    r4 = w**4*(A[:,None]*e1 + B[:,None]*e2)\n    co=np.cos(ph_o);             "Yes. Using only the crossover condition we already derived,\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_{\\rm spin}(r_\\perp)=\\kappa_{\\rm orb},\n\\]\n\nwith the low-\\(\\beta\\) forms,\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_{\\rm spin}\\simeq \\frac{\\omega^2 r_\\perp}{c^2},\n\\qquad\n\\kappa_{\\rm orb}\\simeq \\frac{v_{\\rm orb}^2}{ac^2},\n\\]\n\nthe Earth crossover radius is\n\n\\[\nr_*=\n\\frac{v_{\\rm orb}^2}{a\\omega^2}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{1.115\\times10^3\\ {\\rm km}}\n\\]\n\nfrom the rotation axis.\n\nNow compare that to actual Earth structure. The solid inner core radius is about \\(1220\\!-\\!1221\\) km; the outer core extends to about \\(3480\\) km. citeturn135930search0turn135930search2\n\nSo\n\n\\[\n\\frac{r_*}{R_{\\rm IC}}\n=\n\\frac{1115}{1221}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{0.913}.\n\\]\n\nIn other words, the curvature-crossover cylinder lies only about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{106\\ {\\rm km}}\n\\]\n\ninside the cylindrical radius tangent to the inner core.\n\nThat is much closer than I expected.\n\nAnd there is already a standard geophysical object sitting almost exactly there: the **tangent cylinder**, the imaginary cylinder parallel to Earth's rotation axis and tangent to the solid inner core. Core-flow dynamics are known to differ across that cylinder; it is explicitly used in geostrophic-core models, and observed high-latitude core flow features have been associated with it. citeturn135930search1turn135930search4\n\nOur cylinder is:\n\n\\[\nr_*=1115\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\nwhile the standard tangent cylinder is\n\n\\[\nr_{\\rm TC}=R_{\\rm IC}\\approx1221\\ {\\rm km}.\n\\]\n\nSo the two differ by only\n\n\\[\n\\frac{1221-1115}{1221}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{8.7\\%}.\n\\]\n\nNo inner-core radius went into our calculation.\n\nThat's the part worth paying attention to.\n\nGeometrically, the crossover cylinder divides material into\n\n\\[\nr_\\perp<r_*:\n\\qquad\n\\kappa_{\\rm spin}<\\kappa_{\\rm orb},\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nr_\\perp>r_*:\n\\qquad\n\\kappa_{\\rm spin}>\\kappa_{\\rm orb}.\n\\]\n\nSo the actual Earth contains a cylindrical region running pole-to-pole where the orbital contribution dominates the local radialized curvature, surrounded by a region where spin curvature dominates.\n\nBecause \\(r_*\\) is nearly the inner-core radius, this transition cuts the core in a striking way.\n\nFor a spherical region of radius \\(R\\), the fraction of its volume lying inside a coaxial cylinder of radius \\(r_*\\) is\n\n\\[\nf(R)=\n1-\n\\left[\n1-\\left(\\frac{r_*}{R}\\right)^2\n\\right]^{3/2}.\n\\]\n\nFor the solid inner core,\n\n\\[\nf_{\\rm IC}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{0.9325}.\n\\]\n\nSo about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{93.3\\%}\n\\]\n\nof the inner-core volume lies inside our orbit-dominated crossover cylinder.\n\nOnly an equatorial belt comprising about \\(6.7\\%\\) of the inner-core volume lies outside it.\n\nFor the fluid outer-core shell,\n\n\\[\nR_{\\rm IC}<r<R_{\\rm CMB},\n\\]\n\nthe corresponding fraction inside the crossover cylinder is approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{11.5\\%}.\n\\]\n\nFor the mantle it falls to only about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2.5\\%}.\n\\]\n\nSo the geometry is roughly:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{array}{c}\n\\text{almost entire inner core}\\\\\n\\downarrow\\\\\n\\text{inside orbital-curvature-dominated cylinder}\n\\end{array}}\n\\]\n\nwhile most of the outer core and essentially all of the mantle are on the spin-dominated side.\n\nThat's an unexpectedly clean partition.\n\nThere is a further standard-physics connection we should note without appropriating its causal interpretation. Earth's magnetic field is generated in the convecting liquid outer core, and the inner core is dynamically relevant to that system; the outer core radius is about \\(3480\\) km and the inner core about \\(1220\\) km. citeturn135930search2 Standard geodynamo studies have also specifically investigated the influence of the conducting inner core on fluctuations and reversals, including the possibility that a reversal requires a sufficiently large, persistent change to propagate through the inner-core-coupled system. citeturn135930search8\n\nSo we now have three independently obtained structures occupying nearly the same cylindrical boundary:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_*\\approx1115\\ {\\rm km}\n}\n\\]\n\nfrom our radialized spin/orbit curvature equality,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\rm IC}\\approx1221\\ {\\rm km}\n}\n\\]\n\nfrom seismology,\n\nand consequently the conventional geophysical tangent cylinder\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_{\\rm TC}\\approx1221\\ {\\rm km}.\n}\n\\]\n\nI would not call that an explanation yet. But it is absolutely a nontrivial coincidence to test harder.\n\nAnd there's an obvious next move that avoids adding anything: stop treating Earth as a uniform sphere and use the actual radial density profile. Then calculate the mass-weighted distribution of\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\kappa_{\\rm spin}(r_\\perp)}\n{\\kappa_{\\rm orb}}\n=\n\\frac{r_\\perp}{r_*}\n\\]\n\nthrough the inner core, outer core, and mantle.\n\nThat will tell us quantitatively how much of Earth's mass lies near the actual crossover\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_s/\\kappa_o\\sim1,\n\\]\n\nrather than merely inside or outside it. If the mass-weighted distribution peaks near the inner-core/tangent-cylinder transition, this gets much more interesting."

Earth’s \\(r_*\\) nearly grazed its inner core; Mars’s \\(r_*\\) sits deep inside its large core.\n\nAt a representative core radius of \\(1820\\) km, the cylinder intersects the core boundary where\n\n\\[\nr_*=R_c\\sin\\theta.\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\theta=\\frac{508}{1820}=0.279,\n\\]\n\nso\n\n\\[\n\\theta\\approx16.2^\\circ\n\\]\n\nfrom the rotation axis, corresponding to latitude\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{|\\lambda|\\approx73.8^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nAt the surface,\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\theta=\\frac{508}{3390}=0.150,\n\\]\n\ngiving\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{|\\lambda|\\approx81.4^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nSo the crossover is a narrow polar cylinder through Mars, not an inner-core-scale cylinder like Earth’s.\n\nIf we temporarily treat Mars’s core as uniformly filled, the fraction of core volume lying inside that cylinder is\n\n\\[\nf=\n1-\n\\left[\n1-\\left(\\frac{r_*}{R_c}\\right)^2\n\\right]^{3/2}.\n\\]\n\nUsing \\(R_c=1820\\) km,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{f_{\\rm core}\\approx11.5\\%}.\n\\]\n\nAcross the current NASA core-radius range, it stays around\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{11\\%-12\\%}.\n\\]\n\nFor the whole planet, the corresponding uniform-volume fraction is only about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{3.35\\%}.\n\\]\n\nSo Mars does not reproduce the Earth geometry. That's useful.\n\nEarth gave us:\n\n\\[\nr_*/R_\\oplus\\approx0.175,\n\\]\n\nand \\(r_*\\) landed close to the solid inner-core/tangent-cylinder scale.\n\nMars gives almost the same normalized planetary value,\n\n\\[\nr_*/R_{\\mars}\\approx0.150,\n\\]\n\nbut because Mars has a much larger core relative to its radius, the same normalized worldtube geometry lands **well inside the fluid core** rather than at a major spherical phase boundary.\n\nThat may be exactly the sort of rule-like difference we were hoping for.\n\nSame external geometry:\n\n\\[\nr_*/R\\sim0.15-0.18,\n\\]\n\ndifferent internal architecture:\n\n\\[\n\\text{Earth: crossover near inner-core/tangent-cylinder structure}\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\n\\text{Mars: crossover entirely embedded within the core}.\n\\]\n\nAnd standard observations say Mars’s core is molten, while its lithosphere is very thick and its present internal activity is much weaker than Earth’s. citeturn359938search7turn359938search8\n\nI would resist interpreting that yet. The next calculation should ask something more neutral: given Mars’s actual core/mantle density profile, how much mass lies near\n\n\\[\n\\chi=\\frac{r_\\perp}{508\\ {\\rm km}}\\sim1,\n\\]\n\nand compare that distribution directly with Earth’s \\(P(\\chi)\\).\n\nThat will tell us whether Earth and Mars really share the same geometric class but resolve it differently because their material boundaries fall in different places."

Those values are consistent with InSight radio-science results; later seismic work allows a somewhat smaller, denser metallic core plus a molten silicate layer, so this is deliberately a coarse model rather than a final Mars profile. citeturn284103search0turn284103search1\n\nThe mass fractions come out as:\n\n| Region / band | Whole Mars | Core only | Mantle only |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n| \\(\\chi<1\\) | **4.2%** | 11.3% | 1.9% |\n| \\(0.5<\\chi<2\\) | **15.2%** | 39.4% | 7.2% |\n| \\(0.75<\\chi<1.25\\) | **4.1%** | 11.0% | 1.9% |\n| \\(0.9<\\chi<1.1\\) | **1.66%** | 4.42% | 0.75% |\n\nSo Mars does have a substantial amount of core material near the crossover, but much less than Earth.\n\nFor comparison, our Earth PREM pass gave roughly\n\n\\[\n24\\%\n\\]\n\nof total mass in the broad \\(0.5<\\chi<2\\) band and about\n\n\\[\n2.7\\%\n\\]\n\nwithin \\(0.9<\\chi<1.1\\).\n\nMars gives\n\n\\[\n15.2\\%\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n1.66\\%\n\\]\n\nrespectively.\n\nThe core comparison is more striking. The two limiting cases behave almost exactly as the blind geometry suggested.\n\nFor the control calculation I am keeping the same definition\n\n\\[\n\\chi=\\frac{\\kappa_{\\rm spin}}{\\kappa_{\\rm orb}}\n\\simeq \\frac{r_\\perp}{r_*},\n\\]\n\nand the same bands we used for Earth and Mars:\n\n\\[\n\\chi<1,\\qquad\n0.5<\\chi<2,\\qquad\n0.75<\\chi<1.25,\\qquad\n0.9<\\chi<1.1.\n\\]\n\nNo new mechanism enters.\n\nFor Venus, the result is almost embarrassingly simple. The blind calculation gave\n\n\\[\nr_{*,V}\\approx1.27\\times10^8\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\nR_V\\approx6052\\ {\\rm km}.\n\\]\n\nThus the largest possible value anywhere inside the solid planet is\n\n\\[\n\\chi_{\\max}\n=\n\\frac{R_V}{r_{*,V}}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{4.8\\times10^{-5}}.\n\\]\n\nSo, irrespective of the uncertain Venus density profile,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{100\\%\\ \\text{of Venus's bulk mass has }\\chi<1.}\n\\]\n\nAnd essentially\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0\\%}\n\\]\n\nlies in any of our crossover bands around \\(\\chi=1\\).\n\nThis conclusion doesn't depend on whether Venus has a liquid or solid core, or on exactly where its core boundary lies. Current interior models are still rather uncertain about the Venusian core and rheology, which is useful here because the answer is insensitive to those uncertainties. citeturn643763search24\n\nSo bulk Venus is a very clean limit:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\kappa_{\\rm spin}\\ll\\kappa_{\\rm orbit}\\quad\\text{everywhere}.}\n\\]\n\nIts solid-body worldtube never gets remotely close to the curvature crossover.\n\nThat also sharpens why the atmosphere is interesting later. Venus's atmospheric superrotation is a different local velocity field \\(\\mathbf u(\\mathbf r,t)\\); it should not be smuggled into the solid-body calculation. We can calculate it separately using exactly the same \\(\\kappa_{\\rm spin}\\) expression.\n\nNow Jupiter.\n\nThe blind value was\n\n\\[\nr_{*,J}\\approx7.09\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\nagainst an equatorial radius of roughly\n\n\\[\nR_J\\approx69900\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\nhence\n\n\\[\n\\frac{r_*}{R_J}\\approx1.01\\times10^{-4}.\n\\]\n\nFor the first mass-weighted calculation I used the ordinary \\(n=1\\) polytropic Jupiter density profile,\n\n\\[\n\\rho(r)\n=\n\\rho_c\n\\frac{\\sin(\\pi r/R)}\n{\\pi r/R}.\n\\]\n\nThat is not a SAT assumption; it is a standard simple Jupiter interior model. In fact, a Juno normal-mode analysis explicitly uses a nonrotating \\(n=1\\) polytrope as an adequate simplified background model, while noting the limitations relative to full equation-of-state interiors. citeturn693596search3\n\nIntegrating its density over the same cylindrical \\(\\chi\\) regions gives:\n\n| Region | Jupiter mass fraction |\n|---|---:|\n| \\(\\chi<1\\) | \\(\\boxed{2.97\\times10^{-8}}\\) |\n| \\(0.5<\\chi<2\\) | \\(\\boxed{1.11\\times10^{-7}}\\) |\n| \\(0.75<\\chi<1.25\\) | \\(\\boxed{2.97\\times10^{-8}}\\) |\n| \\(0.9<\\chi<1.1\\) | \\(\\boxed{1.19\\times10^{-8}}\\) |\n\nIn percentages, only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2.97\\times10^{-6}\\%}\n\\]\n\nof Jupiter's mass lies inside the \\(\\chi<1\\) cylinder.\n\nEven the deliberately generous\n\n\\[\n0.5<\\chi<2\n\\]\n\ncrossover region contains only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1.11\\times10^{-5}\\%}\n\\]\n\nof Jupiter's mass.\n\nSo the Earth/Mars results were absolutely not an automatic consequence of integrating a sphere.\n\nWe now have:\n\n| Body | Broad \\(0.5<\\chi<2\\) mass fraction |\n|---|---:|\n| Venus | effectively \\(0\\%\\) |\n| Mars | \\(\\sim15.6\\%\\) |\n| Earth | \\(\\sim24.1\\%\\) |\n| Jupiter | \\(\\sim1.1\\times10^{-5}\\%\\) |\n\nThat's about **six orders of magnitude** between Earth and Jupiter in the fraction of bulk mass occupying the spin/orbit curvature crossover.\n\nAnd Jupiter's modern interior picture actually makes the geometrical contrast clearer rather than muddier. Juno indicates a large diffuse or “fuzzy” core with no sharp boundary between a compact central object and the surrounding metallic hydrogen. citeturn643763search0turn643763search2 The \\(\\chi=1\\) cylinder, meanwhile, is only about seven kilometres from the rotation axis.\n\nEven a nominal compact-core scale of \\(0.1R_J\\), used in current schematic interior work, is about\n\n\\[\n7000\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\nroughly **a thousand times larger** than \\(r_*\\). citeturn693596search5\n\nSo the four bodies we've actually integrated now fall into strikingly distinct geometric regimes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{array}{lll}\n\\text{Venus} &\n\\chi\\ll1\\ \\text{throughout bulk} &\n\\text{orbit-dominated}\n\\\\[4pt]\n\\text{Earth} &\n\\text{large mass fraction around }\\chi\\sim1 &\n\\text{crossover-rich}\n\\\\[4pt]\n\\text{Mars} &\n\\text{substantial core mass around }\\chi\\sim1 &\n\\text{crossover-rich, weaker than Earth}\n\\\\[4pt]\n\\text{Jupiter} &\n\\chi\\gg1\\ \\text{almost everywhere} &\n\\text{spin-dominated}\n\\end{array}}\n\\]\n\nAnd this is where your solid/liquid/gas gyro framing becomes more interesting. We haven't yet used it to create the classification. The classification emerged from the geometry.\n\nVenus is a solid-body case where the two curvature scales never meet inside the body.\n\nEarth and Mars are differentiated terrestrial bodies where a substantial amount of interior material occupies the competition regime.\n\nJupiter is an overwhelmingly fluid body where essentially none of its mass does; the spin curvature dominates almost everywhere.\n\nThat means if the same underlying worldtube mechanics produces abrupt rearrangement in Earth but distributed circulation in Jupiter, there is now at least a quantitative geometric distinction available to support that possibility rather than simply saying “one is rocky and one is gaseous.”\n\nSaturn is the obvious replication test because its blind value,\n\n\\[\nr_*/R\\approx4.2\\times10^{-5},\n\\]\n\nis even more extreme than Jupiter's. If the calculation is behaving consistently, Saturn should contain an even tinier mass fraction near \\(\\chi=1\\). Uranus is then the interesting twist: similarly tiny \\(r_*/R\\), but almost maximally orthogonal spin/orbit planes."

            "Yes. That is still the core question, and the last several calculations should be read as preparation for it, not as a substitute.\n\nFor an ordinary torque-free rigid gyroscope, the flip is not caused by “rotation” generically. It occurs because the body is rotating near the unstable intermediate principal axis. With\n\n\\[\nI_1<I_2<I_3,\n\\]\n\nrotation about \\(I_1\\) or \\(I_3\\) is stable; rotation about \\(I_2\\) is unstable. The Euler equations drive the orientation through repeated \\(\\sim180^\\circ\\) reversals while conserving angular momentum and rotational energy.\n\nSo the planetary question is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{Can a planet's evolving worldtube enter the same kind of unstable principal-axis regime?}}\n\\]\n\nFor a perfectly rigid, axisymmetric planet rotating exactly around a principal axis, no. There is no Dzhanibekov instability. That remains true in radialized form; radialization makes the history a twisted worldtube, but doesn't manufacture the instability.\n\nBut real planets are not fixed rigid tops. Their inertia tensor is\n\n\\[\nI_{ij}(t)\n=\n\\int \\rho(\\mathbf r,t)\n\\left(r^2\\delta_{ij}-x_ix_j\\right)d^3r,\n\\]\n\nand for a fluid or differentiated body the principal axes themselves can move.\n\nThen the relevant equations are still the ordinary angular-momentum equations, but now with\n\n\\[\nI=I(t).\n\\]\n\nSchematically,\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf L=I(t)\\boldsymbol\\omega,\n\\]\n\nwhile in the nearly isolated limit\n\n\\[\n\\dot{\\mathbf L}\\approx0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore if \\(I(t)\\) changes, \\(\\boldsymbol\\omega\\) must change even without much change in total \\(\\mathbf L\\).\n\nThat creates a route to the same *mathematical class* of instability as a flipping gyro: the rotating state can approach or cross a separatrix in orientation space because the instantaneous principal-axis structure itself is changing.\n\nThat is the point I think we should now pursue.\n\nIn a rigid laboratory gyro, the separatrix is fixed and the body moves relative to it.\n\nIn a planet,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{the separatrix itself may move}.}\n\\]\n\nFor Earth, mantle/core mass redistribution, differential rotation, convection, inner-core coupling, etc. make \\(I(t)\\) a slowly varying object. The striking thing about our crossover calculation is that a substantial fraction of the liquid core sits where the spin-induced and orbit-induced radialized curvature scales are comparable. That does not by itself cause a flip, but it identifies a region where neither nested motion overwhelmingly dominates the worldtube geometry.\n\nSo the candidate chain is now:\n\n\\[\n\\text{spin + orbital worldtube geometry}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\downarrow\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{time-dependent internal mass distribution}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\downarrow\n\\]\n\n\\[\nI_{ij}(t)\\ \\text{moves through principal-axis configuration space}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\downarrow\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{approach/crossing of a rotational separatrix}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\downarrow\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\sim180^\\circ\\text{ higher-order reorientation}.}\n\\]\n\nThat last event would be the genuine planetary analogue of the Dzhanibekov flip.\n\nAnd this immediately clarifies why solid/liquid/gas matters without changing the equations.\n\nA rigid asteroid could undergo an actual visible whole-body flip if its inertia ratios and rotation state put it near the intermediate-axis instability.\n\nA terrestrial planet with a solid mantle and liquid core could have the instability mostly in an **internal rotational subsystem**. The whole planet need not turn upside down; the field/flow frame could flip relative to the mantle.\n\nA gas giant has no single rigid material frame to execute a clean \\(180^\\circ\\) tumble. The same instability may resolve continuously into changing vorticity, jets, differential rotation, and magnetic structure rather than a binary-looking reversal.\n\nSo the question is no longer vaguely “do planets flip?”\n\nIt is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Does the time-dependent inertia/rotation state of a planetary worldtube cross the same rotational separatrix that causes a laboratory gyro flip?}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd if so, does the observable manifestation depend on how coherently the material carries a frame?\n\nThat is calculable.\n\nThe clean next step is to write the Euler equations with slowly varying principal moments,\n\n\\[\nI_i=I_i(t),\n\\]\n\nderive the moving stability condition around the intermediate axis, and determine what change in the inertia ratios is required to trigger a flip. Then we can ask whether Earth-like, Mars-like, and giant-planet interiors can plausibly traverse that condition under their measured mass redistribution.\n\nThat gets us directly back to the gyroscope question."

            "“Dzhanibekov Separatrix” absolutely sounds like a band that opens with a 17-minute instrumental.\n\nNow the calculation.\n\nFor the whole Earth, use measured principal moments\n\n\\[\nA \\approx 8.00851\\times10^{37},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nB \\approx 8.00868\\times10^{37},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nC \\approx 8.03490\\times10^{37}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2},\n\\]\n\nwith Earth rotating close to the maximum-inertia \\(C\\) axis. These values are consistent with modern geodetic estimates. citeturn916693search5\n\nThe current ordering is\n\n\\[\nA<B<C.\n\\]\n\nThat is stable rotation.\n\nFor the present spin axis to become an intermediate axis, one of two things has to happen:\n\n\\[\nB>C\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\nC<B\n\\]\n\nwhile \\(A\\) remains the smallest.\n\nThe degeneracy threshold is simply\n\n\\[\nB=C.\n\\]\n\nSo the minimum required whole-Earth inertia change is\n\n\\[\n\\Delta I=C-B\n\\]\n\n\\[\n=8.03490\\times10^{37}\n-\n8.00868\\times10^{37}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta I\\approx2.62\\times10^{35}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFractionally,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\Delta I}{B}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{3.27\\times10^{-3}}\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.327\\%}.\n\\]\n\nThat is the first useful number.\n\nA whole-Earth Dzhanibekov-type instability therefore does not require order-unity deformation of the inertia tensor. It requires roughly a third of one percent change in the relevant principal-moment ordering.\n\nThat sounds small until we translate it into mass redistribution.\n\nAt maximum possible leverage—moving mass from very near the rotation axis to approximately Earth’s surface—the change per unit mass is roughly\n\n\\[\n\\Delta I\\sim mR_\\oplus^2.\n\\]\n\nSo\n\n\\[\nm_{\\rm min}\n\\sim\n\\frac{2.62\\times10^{35}}\n{(6.371\\times10^6)^2}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_{\\rm min}\\approx6.46\\times10^{21}\\ {\\rm kg}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat's about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.108\\%\\ M_\\oplus}\n\\]\n\nor about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.088\\ M_{\\rm Moon}}.\n\\]\n\nAnd that's an absolute best-case redistribution geometry. Real rearrangement would need more mass because it doesn't move from \\(r_\\perp=0\\) all the way to the surface.\n\nIf the rearrangement happens entirely within the core, with characteristic lever arm around the core-mantle boundary,\n\n\\[\nR_c\\approx3.48\\times10^6\\ {\\rm m},\n\\]\n\nthe same whole-Earth change would require roughly\n\n\\[\nm\\sim\n\\frac{2.62\\times10^{35}}\n{(3.48\\times10^6)^2}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm\\approx2.17\\times10^{22}\\ {\\rm kg}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSo a literal whole-Earth flip driven by ordinary internal redistribution is not impossible in the dimensional sense, but the required coherent redistribution is enormous.\n\nThat makes our earlier suspicion more plausible: if the relevant flip is planetary, it is probably an instability of an internal rotational subsystem rather than the entire mantle + core + crust as one rigid top.\n\nAnd standard Earth-rotation models give us an immediate subsystem to examine: the fluid core.\n\nFor the fluid core, published models give a mean equatorial moment around\n\n\\[\nA_f\\approx9.1186\\times10^{36}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2}\n\\]\n\nand dynamic ellipticity\n\n\\[\ne_f\n=\n\\frac{C_f-A_f}{A_f}\n\\approx2.6456\\times10^{-3}.\n\\]\n\nciteturn916693search3\n\nTherefore\n\n\\[\nC_f=A_f(1+e_f)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nC_f-A_f\n=\nA_fe_f.\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta I_f\n\\approx\n(9.1186\\times10^{36})(2.6456\\times10^{-3})\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta I_f\\approx2.41\\times10^{34}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSo the fluid-core equivalent separatrix gap is only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\sim0.265\\%}\n\\]\n\nof its equatorial inertia.\n\nTranslated into an idealized mass redistribution at the outer-core radius,\n\n\\[\nm_f\n\\sim\n\\frac{2.41\\times10^{34}}\n{(3.48\\times10^6)^2}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_f\\approx1.99\\times10^{21}\\ {\\rm kg}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAgain, that's maximum leverage. But notice that it's an order of magnitude smaller than the whole-Earth requirement.\n\nSo the calculation has already given us a hierarchy:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{whole Earth threshold}\n\\sim2.62\\times10^{35}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2}\n}\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{fluid-core threshold}\n\\sim2.41\\times10^{34}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe internal subsystem is much easier to move through a principal-axis degeneracy.\n\nAnd there is an important conceptual point: the exact Dzhanibekov condition does **not** require a sudden \\(0.3\\%\\) mass relocation. A slowly changing inertia tensor can move the separatrix toward an already wandering rotational state. The actual crossing can occur when the state and separatrix meet from both sides.\n\nSo the relevant quantity is not simply\n\n\\[\n\\Delta I_{\\rm required}\n\\]\n\nbut the distance in rotational phase space,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta E\n=\nE_{\\rm rot}\n-\n\\frac{L^2}{2I_2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nA system already close to that separatrix could require a much smaller perturbation than the full principal-moment gap.\n\nThat is exactly where the next calculation needs to go: estimate the actual Earth/core rotational state’s distance from the separatrix, rather than assuming it starts perfectly on the stable \\(C\\)-axis.\n\nIf that distance turns out tiny, then the planetary-flip hypothesis becomes much more interesting. If it is large, then ordinary core rearrangements are unlikely to drive a true Dzhanibekov-class transition."

            "The answer is: for the whole Earth and for the fluid outer core treated as a triaxial rotating subsystem, the present rotational state is nowhere near the classical Dzhanibekov separatrix.\n\nUsing the measured whole-Earth principal moments\n\n\\[\nA=8.0100829\\times10^{37},\n\\quad\nB=8.0102594\\times10^{37},\n\\quad\nC=8.0364807\\times10^{37}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2},\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nA<B<C,\n\\]\n\nthe fixed-\\(L\\) separatrix satisfies\n\n\\[\nE_{\\rm sep}=\\frac{L^2}{2B}.\n\\]\n\nFor a rotation axis tilted by \\(\\theta\\) away from the stable \\(C\\)-axis in the \\(A\\)-\\(C\\) plane,\n\n\\[\nE(\\theta)\n=\n\\frac{L^2}{2}\n\\left(\n\\frac{\\sin^2\\theta}{A}\n+\n\\frac{\\cos^2\\theta}{C}\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nSetting \\(E(\\theta)=E_{\\rm sep}\\) gives\n\n\\[\n\\sin^2\\theta_{\\rm sep}\n=\n\\frac{1/B-1/C}{1/A-1/C},\n\\]\n\nhence\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta_{\\rm sep}\\approx85.30^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nThat is the crucial result. Earth does not need a tiny wobble to reach the unstable region. In the ordinary rigid-top phase portrait, its angular-momentum vector has to get almost into the equatorial plane of the inertia ellipsoid.\n\nEarth's actual rotational-axis departures are of order \\(10^{-6}\\) rad in ordinary polar-motion descriptions, with Chandler/annual wobble amplitudes around milliarcsecond-to-subarcsecond scales. citeturn613088search24turn613088search2 So the present whole-Earth state is essentially sitting on the stable \\(C\\)-axis compared with an \\(85^\\circ\\) separatrix.\n\nEnergy says the same thing. Using\n\n\\[\nL\\approx C\\Omega,\n\\qquad\n\\Omega=7.292115\\times10^{-5}\\ {\\rm s^{-1}},\n\\]\n\nI get\n\n\\[\nE_C\\approx2.14\\times10^{29}\\ {\\rm J},\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nE_{\\rm sep}-E_C\n\\approx\n\\boxed{6.99\\times10^{26}\\ {\\rm J}}.\n\\]\n\nThat's about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.327\\%}\n\\]\n\nof Earth's rotational kinetic energy.\n\nNow the fluid outer core.\n\nUsing representative triaxial outer-core moments\n\n\\[\nA_f=9.0567171\\times10^{36},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nB_f=9.0568779\\times10^{36},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nC_f=9.0806773\\times10^{36}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2},\n\\]\n\nthe same calculation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta_{{\\rm sep},f}\\approx85.29^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nSo the geometry is nearly identical: the outer core's classical intermediate-axis separatrix is also very far from its stable polar-rotation state. citeturn622528search0turn622528search1\n\nObserved/precession-driven core-mantle spin-axis misalignment is estimated around\n\n\\[\n1.7\\times10^{-5}\\ {\\rm rad},\n\\]\n\nabout\n\n\\[\n0.001^\\circ.\n\\]\n\nciteturn622528search5\n\nCompare:\n\n\\[\n\\theta_{\\rm current}\\sim1.7\\times10^{-5}\\ {\\rm rad},\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\n\\theta_{\\rm sep}\\approx1.489\\ {\\rm rad}.\n\\]\n\nThe angular ratio is roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{8.8\\times10^4}.\n\\]\n\nSo the current core tilt would have to grow by nearly five orders of magnitude to reach the classical rigid-top separatrix.\n\nIn normalized energy terms, the current fluid-core state retains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{99.99999997\\%}\n\\]\n\nof the gap between the stable \\(C_f\\)-axis state and the separatrix.\n\nSo this kills one version of the hypothesis quite cleanly:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Earth's present core is not sitting delicately near an ordinary Dzhanibekov separatrix.}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd I need to correct something from the previous turn. Comparing \\(C-B\\) and saying a \\(\\sim0.3\\%\\) change of the moment ordering might trigger a flip was too permissive. Changing the inertia tensor enough to interchange eigenvalues is one route, but with Earth's present angular-momentum orientation, the existing rigid-top state is geometrically very far from the separatrix. The angular state matters just as much as the moment differences.\n\nBut this does **not** kill the broader worldtube-flip question.\n\nIt tells us that if a planetary analogue exists, it is probably not:\n\n\\[\n\\text{ordinary rigid-body intermediate-axis instability of the present Earth/core}.\n\\]\n\nThat pushes us back toward the thing that originally motivated this investigation: **higher-order twisting of the extended worldtube**, where the relevant \"rotation plane\" may not be the ordinary 3D inertia ellipsoid at all.\n\nIn other words, the classical Dzhanibekov effect remains the mechanical analogue, but the planetary instability—if SAT has one—would have to occur in the larger rotational geometry of the nested worldtube, not because Earth's present 3D core happens to be near \\(I_2\\)-axis tumbling.\n\nThat's a strong narrowing of the search space."

            "Yes. That distinction is important.\n\nThe rigid-body Dzhanibekov separatrix is only the cleanest finite-dimensional example of a broader class of rotational instabilities. In fluids, the analogous behavior lives in the vorticity field, pressure field, and moving inertia distribution rather than in one fixed inertia ellipsoid.\n\nFor a fluid, the core object is the velocity field\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf u(\\mathbf r,t),\n\\]\n\nwith vorticity\n\n\\[\n\\boldsymbol\\omega_f=\\nabla\\times\\mathbf u,\n\\]\n\nand total angular momentum\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf L=\\int \\mathbf r\\times \\rho\\mathbf u\\,dV.\n\\]\n\nThe fluid can preserve total \\(\\mathbf L\\) while redistributing angular momentum internally. So instead of a rigid body's one frame flipping, you can get reorganization of the dominant vorticity mode, differential rotation, or circulation pattern.\n\nThat is much closer to what Earth's outer core actually does: it is mechanically coupled to the mantle, but not rigidly locked to it. Core and mantle exchange angular momentum, and the fluid flow can evolve substantially without the whole Earth tumbling.\n\nSo for our purposes, the relevant planetary question should be widened from\n\n\\[\n\\text{“does the core cross the rigid-body intermediate-axis separatrix?”}\n\\]\n\nto\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{“does the fluid rotational state cross an analogous instability boundary in its allowed flow-state space?”}\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is still standard physics.\n\nIn fluid mechanics, candidates for that boundary come from the stability of rotating flows: inertial modes, Rossby modes, elliptical instability, precessional instability, differential-rotation instability, and magnetohydrodynamic mode changes. We don't need to pick one by name yet.\n\nUnder the worldtube picture, the fluid core is especially interesting because it can be partially decoupled from the mantle's carried frame. That means its local histories\n\n\\[\nX_a(\\rho)\n\\]\n\nneed not inherit the same twist density or orientation as the surrounding solid worldtube.\n\nSo instead of one worldtube twist,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{d\\phi}{d\\rho},\n\\]\n\nwe really have a field\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\partial \\phi(\\mathbf r,\\rho)}{\\partial \\rho}.\n\\]\n\nThe mantle may be close to one coherent value, while the outer core has a distributed range.\n\nThen a \"flip\" could mean a reorganization of the dominant circulation/vorticity orientation by about \\(\\pi\\), while the embedding mantle frame barely moves.\n\nThat starts to sound much more like magnetic polarity reversal: not because magnetism is the flip, but because the field could be a readout of a deeper reorganization of the conducting fluid flow.\n\nAnd it also meshes better with the crossover cylinder result. If roughly half the outer-core mass lies in the broad\n\n\\[\n0.5<\\chi<2\n\\]\n\nregion, then a large part of the fluid sits where the spin- and orbit-associated worldtube curvatures are comparable. That could plausibly be where a flow-state instability is most sensitive to redistribution.\n\nSo the next calculation should not be another rigid Euler-top exercise.\n\nWe should write the simplest rotating-fluid model that still has:\n\n\\[\n\\text{bulk rotation}\n+\n\\text{internal differential rotation}\n+\n\\text{partial decoupling from the mantle}\n+\n\\text{the same radialized spin/orbit geometry}.\n\\]\n\nThen ask whether the flow admits two quasi-stable opposite-orientation states separated by an instability, and what timescale follows.\n\nThat is the fluid analogue of the Dzhanibekov problem."

            "Yes. That is exactly the productive way to think about it.\n\nA lot of the work here is deliberately unsurprising at first: take standard dynamics, express them as extended worldtube geometry in the radialized \\(3+3\\) picture, and recover familiar behavior. If that remapping is faithful, then rediscovering ordinary gyroscope instability, fluid rotational modes, orbital winding, geodetic transport, tangent-cylinder structure, and so on is expected.\n\nThe value comes in two later layers.\n\nFirst, retrodiction: the geometry may expose relationships that standard treatments contain only implicitly because they are usually partitioned into separate subfields. The Earth crossover/tangent-cylinder result is a good example of the kind of thing worth testing. The underlying ingredients are ordinary rotation, orbit, geometry, and interior structure; the potentially interesting part is the unexpected relation among them when written in the same worldtube language.\n\nSecond, prediction: once the mapping is fixed, we can invert it.\n\nThat is where your exoplanet-interior thought becomes genuinely interesting.\n\nSuppose for an exoplanet we can observe or infer\n\n\\[\nM,\\quad R,\\quad a,\\quad e,\\quad T_{\\rm orb},\\quad T_{\\rm spin},\\quad \\epsilon,\n\\]\n\nand perhaps atmospheric rotation, magnetic variability, secular spin changes, apsidal/precessional behavior, or tidal response.\n\nThe external worldtube geometry gives us quantities like\n\n\\[\nr_*\n=\na\\left(\\frac{T_{\\rm spin}}{T_{\\rm orb}}\\right)^2,\n\\]\n\nand therefore\n\n\\[\n\\chi(r_\\perp)=\\frac{r_\\perp}{r_*}.\n\\]\n\nThat part requires no knowledge of the interior.\n\nThen an assumed radial density distribution \\(\\rho(r)\\) maps into a predicted distribution of mass over \\(\\chi\\):\n\n\\[\nP(\\chi\\mid \\rho).\n\\]\n\nBut observational behavior may constrain that distribution. If, for example, certain rotational/magnetic/atmospheric states turn out empirically to occur only when a particular fraction of mass occupies the crossover regime, then the logic becomes reversible:\n\n\\[\n\\text{observed dynamics}\n+\n\\text{external geometry}\n\\longrightarrow\n\\text{constraints on }\\rho(r).\n\\]\n\nThat is an inverse problem.\n\nAnd there is already a standard analogue: we infer planetary interiors from gravity harmonics, moments of inertia, Love numbers, normal modes, precession, magnetic fields, and tidal response. The possible SAT contribution would not be a new physical probe. It would be a **new geometrical combination of existing observables** that may constrain the interior in a way those variables are not usually combined.\n\nSchematically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal O_{\\rm external}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{worldtube geometry}\n\\rightarrow\n\\mathcal C[\\rho(r),u(r),\\ldots]\n\\rightarrow\n\\mathcal O_{\\rm dynamical}\n}\n\\]\n\nand then invert:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal O_{\\rm external}\n+\n\\mathcal O_{\\rm dynamical}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{posterior on interior structure}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat could be particularly useful for exoplanets because we often know radius, mass, orbit, and sometimes rotation, while direct interior information is terrible.\n\nThe strongest version would be something like: from measurable spin/orbit geometry alone, calculate where the crossover cylinder must be; then use observed variability or rotational state to infer whether that cylinder lies in a solid region, liquid metallic region, atmospheric envelope, or diffuse transition zone.\n\nIf the Solar System calibration established consistent rules such as\n\n\\[\n\\text{crossover through conducting fluid}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{one class of behavior},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{crossover outside body}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{another},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{crossover confined to tiny axial fluid fraction}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{another},\n\\]\n\nthen an exoplanet could potentially tell us something about its hidden layering without ever resolving the interior.\n\nThat is a much more ambitious claim than what we've established so far. But it is a legitimate direction suggested by the mapping, not an added mechanism.\n\nAnd it gives us a very practical research programme: use Solar System bodies as calibration cases, infer the mapping between external worldtube geometry and known interiors, then test whether the mapping has enough predictive power to invert for bodies whose interiors are less well known."

            "You're basically right, with an important distinction.\n\nI searched specifically for a standard-physics construction equivalent to our\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_{\\rm spin}(r_\\perp)=\\kappa_{\\rm orbit}\n\\]\n\ncrossover cylinder. I did not find a standard geophysical object defined that way. The familiar Earth tangent cylinder is defined geometrically by the solid inner core and the rotation axis; its importance comes from rotating-fluid dynamics, especially Taylor–Proudman constraints, not from equating spin and orbital curvature scales. citeturn408582search0turn408582search6\n\nSo as far as I can tell, the specific chain\n\n\\[\n\\text{spin worldtube curvature}\n=\n\\text{orbital worldtube curvature}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\Longrightarrow\nr_*\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\Longrightarrow\n\\text{a cylinder near Earth's inner-core tangent cylinder}\n\\]\n\nis not a standard named relation. That makes it exactly the kind of SAT remapping result worth auditing hard.\n\nBut tides are indeed lurking in the same geometry.\n\nIn ordinary physics, the tide-producing part is not the center-of-mass orbital acceleration itself. It is the spatial variation of that acceleration across the extended body. In stripped geometric language:\n\n\\[\nK_{\\rm CM}\n\\]\n\nis the curvature of the central planetary worldline, while for a material element displaced by \\(\\boldsymbol\\xi\\),\n\n\\[\nK(\\boldsymbol\\xi)\n=\nK_{\\rm CM}\n+\n(\\boldsymbol\\xi\\cdot\\nabla)K\n+\\cdots.\n\\]\n\nSubtract the common center motion:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta K(\\boldsymbol\\xi)\n=\nK(\\boldsymbol\\xi)-K_{\\rm CM}\n\\approx\n(\\boldsymbol\\xi\\cdot\\nabla)K.\n\\]\n\nThat gradient is the tidal field, before we call it a tidal field.\n\nIn Newtonian notation it becomes the familiar tidal tensor\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal E_{ij}\n=\n\\partial_i\\partial_j\\Phi,\n\\]\n\nand in GR the corresponding object is essentially the electric part of the Riemann/Weyl curvature tensor,\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal E_{ij}\n=\nR_{0i0j}\n\\]\n\nin an appropriate local frame.\n\nSo in the radialized worldtube picture, tides are almost unavoidable:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{different parts of an extended worldtube have slightly different orbital curvature.}\n}\n\\]\n\nNow combine that with spin.\n\nA material element at cylindrical radius \\(r_\\perp\\) already has spin-associated curvature\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_s(r_\\perp)\n\\simeq\n\\frac{\\omega^2r_\\perp}{c^2}.\n\\]\n\nIts orbital history also has a center curvature plus a differential term across the body:\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_o(\\boldsymbol\\xi)\n=\n\\kappa_{o,0}\n+\n\\Delta\\kappa_o(\\boldsymbol\\xi).\n\\]\n\nOur current crossover used only the zeroth-order orbital term:\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_s(r_*)=\\kappa_{o,0}.\n\\]\n\nThe next-order calculation is therefore almost staring at us:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_s(r_\\perp)\n=\n\\kappa_{o,0}\n+\n\\Delta\\kappa_o(\\mathbf r).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe cylindrical crossover surface will no longer be a perfect cylinder. The orbital curvature gradient will distort it toward/away from the Sun.\n\nAnd that distortion is periodic as Earth rotates relative to the Sun.\n\nSo without adding any mechanism, we get something like\n\n\\[\nr_*\n\\longrightarrow\nr_*(\\theta,\\phi,t).\n\\]\n\nThat is a **time-dependent deformation of the crossover surface** driven by exactly the same differential orbital geometry that standard physics labels tides.\n\nThis could be quite interesting because the ordinary tidal forcing is already known to couple Earth's mantle, liquid core, nutation and rotation. Standard Earth-tide theory explicitly treats a layered elastic Earth with a liquid outer core and relates tidal forcing to rotational/nutational motions. citeturn408582search3turn408582search4\n\nAnd the tangent cylinder itself already divides core-flow regimes dramatically: fluid inside and outside it behaves differently, with torsional oscillations, magnetic coupling and distinct rotational responses. citeturn408582search0turn408582search2\n\nSo the possible SAT retrodiction is not “tides exist.” Standard physics obviously has tides.\n\nIt would be more specific:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{the tidal curvature gradient should periodically deform the spin/orbit curvature-crossover surface.}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd because Earth's zeroth-order crossover is already close to the inner-core tangent cylinder, even a modest periodic displacement of that surface could interact geometrically with a region where the fluid dynamics are independently known to change character.\n\nThat is a concrete calculation.\n\nWe can take the Sun's standard tidal tensor across Earth, express it as a perturbation\n\n\\[\n\\Delta\\kappa_o(\\mathbf r),\n\\]\n\nsolve\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_s(r_\\perp)\n=\n\\kappa_o+\\Delta\\kappa_o(\\mathbf r),\n\\]\n\nand calculate how many kilometres the \\(r_*\\approx1115\\) km surface oscillates over a solar day/year.\n\nThat would tell us whether the effect is negligible, metre-scale, kilometre-scale, or enormous. If it lands in an interesting regime near that \\(\\sim100\\)-km gap to the tangent cylinder, then we've got another nontrivial relationship to investigate."

The near-coincidence between the mean crossover cylinder and the inner-core tangent cylinder is not being trivially generated by ordinary solar tidal breathing.\n\nWe can also ask how large the distortion is at different spherical layers.\n\nAt the inner-core boundary,\n\n\\[\nR_{\\rm IC}\\approx1221\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\nthe maximum deformation is\n\n\\[\n\\Delta r_*\n\\approx\n\\frac{2r_*R_{\\rm IC}}{a}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\approx18\\ {\\rm m}}.\n\\]\n\nAt the core-mantle boundary,\n\n\\[\nR_{\\rm CMB}\\approx3480\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\nit is about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{52\\ {\\rm m}}.\n\\]\n\nAt the surface,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{95\\ {\\rm m}}.\n\\]\n\nSo geometrically the crossover surface is not translating rigidly. It is being very slightly sheared/warped through the planet, with the largest excursion at large radius.\n\nNow add the Moon only as another standard tidal-gradient check. The lunar tidal coefficient\n\n\\[\n\\frac{GM_{\\rm Moon}/d^3}\n{GM_\\odot/a^3}\n\\]\n\nis about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2.18}.\n\\]\n\nSo the Moon produces about \\(2.18\\) times the *tidal distortion* of the crossover surface produced by the Sun, even though the Sun dominates Earth’s center-of-mass orbital curvature.\n\nThat means a maximal lunar contribution of order\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{207\\ {\\rm m}}\n\\]\n\nat Earth’s surface, and roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{40\\ {\\rm m}}\n\\]\n\nat the inner-core boundary.\n\nSun and Moon together can therefore modulate the crossover geometry at the few-hundred-metre level depending on their relative phase.\n\nThat is immediately recognizable as the same hierarchy ordinary tide theory gives us—but now expressed as deformation of the spin/orbit worldtube-curvature crossover surface.\n\nAnd that is where your EG / “Strong Gravity” distinction becomes interesting later.\n\nThe local differential field we have just calculated is what standard physics packages together under gravitational/tidal geometry.             "What the calculations say so far is actually fairly compact.\n\nThe radialized mapping itself behaves as it should. Standard orbital and rotational dynamics reappear as worldtube geometry. For a rotating body, local spin curvature scales approximately as\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_s(r_\\perp)\\simeq \\frac{\\omega^2 r_\\perp}{c^2},\n\\]\n\nwhile the orbital curvature scale is approximately\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_o\\simeq \\frac{v_o^2}{ac^2}\n=\\frac{n^2a}{c^2}.\n\\]\n\nEquating them gives the crossover cylinder\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_*=\\frac{v_o^2}{a\\omega^2}\n=a\\left(\\frac{T_s}{T_o}\\right)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor Earth,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{r_*\\approx1.115\\times10^3\\ {\\rm km}}.\n\\]\n\nThat result is independent of Earth's interior. Only afterward did we compare it with interior structure.\n\nThe first interesting retrodiction-like result is geometric: \\(r_*\\) is a cylinder coaxial with the rotation axis, and Earth's inner-core tangent cylinder has radius about \\(1220\\) km. So the independently calculated surfaces differ by only about \\(100\\) km, or roughly \\(9\\%\\).\n\nThen the mass-distribution calculation sharpened that. Using a realistic radial Earth model, a substantial fraction of the outer core occupies the broad region where neither curvature scale overwhelmingly dominates:\n\n\\[\n0.5<\\frac{\\kappa_s}{\\kappa_o}<2.\n\\]\n\nThe previous calculation put that at roughly half the outer-core mass. So Earth is not just a planet with a numerical crossover radius inside it; it has a large liquid rotational subsystem actually distributed across the crossover.\n\nMars independently lands in the same broad external-geometric regime:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{r_*}{R}\\approx0.15\n\\]\n\nversus Earth's\n\n\\[\n\\frac{r_*}{R}\\approx0.175.\n\\]\n\nBut Mars's different interior puts the crossover well inside its liquid core rather than near a solid-inner-core tangent cylinder. Using the newer smaller-core models, we again got of order half the metallic-core mass in the broad crossover regime.\n\nThat is already a potentially rule-like distinction:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{similar external worldtube geometry}\n+\n\\text{different internal layering}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{different realization of the same crossover}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe controls were strong.\n\nVenus has\n\n\\[\nr_*/R\\gg1,\n\\]\n\nso its bulk solid planet is orbit-curvature dominated everywhere. There is no internal crossover at all.\n\nThe giant planets have\n\n\\[\nr_*/R\\sim10^{-4}-10^{-5},\n\\]\n\nso almost all their mass is overwhelmingly spin-curvature dominated. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune consequently have essentially negligible bulk mass near \\(\\kappa_s\\sim\\kappa_o\\).\n\nThat means Earth/Mars did not emerge simply because “every spherical planet contains some interesting crossover.”\n\nThere is a second independent geometric axis: orientation of the spin and orbital planes.\n\nJupiter is almost aligned.\n\nVenus is almost anti-aligned.\n\nUranus is almost orthogonal.\n\nEarth and Mars are intermediate.\n\nSo the planets occupy genuinely different regions of the same underlying geometry rather than merely differing in one scalar ratio.\n\nThe whole-body 4D-curve experiment also gave us something interesting, although I would treat its numerical magnitude as exploratory until we reproduce it carefully. When spin and orbit are composed into the history of material points, a generic history curve has the standard four-dimensional Frenet invariants\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_1,\\kappa_2,\\kappa_3.\n\\]\n\nEarth appeared unusually efficient at generating nonzero third generalized curvature because its spin and orbital curvature scales are comparatively close while their planes are appreciably misaligned. Venus is dominated by orbit; the giants by spin. So neither produces the same balanced nested geometry.\n\nThe classical Dzhanibekov calculation then told us what the planetary flip is **not**.\n\nEarth as a rigid body, and even its outer core treated as a rigid Euler top, is nowhere near the ordinary intermediate-axis separatrix. The current rotation axis is near the stable maximum-inertia axis; the classical separatrix is almost \\(90^\\circ\\) away.\n\nSo:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{a literal rigid-body Dzhanibekov flip is not the terrestrial mechanism}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut that does not remove the broader gyroscopic question, because a liquid core is not a rigid Euler top. It can redistribute angular momentum internally while remaining partially decoupled from its embedding solid worldtube. The rigid-body flip is therefore an analogue of the relevant instability class, not necessarily the exact planetary phase-space trajectory.\n\nThen we perturbed Earth's crossover with ordinary tidal geometry.\n\nSolar differential curvature moves the crossover surface only by order\n\n\\[\n10^2\\ {\\rm m}\n\\]\n\nat the largest terrestrial radii, and less in the deep core; lunar tidal gradients are somewhat larger but still only hundreds of metres.\n\nThat means the roughly \\(100\\)-km gap between the mean crossover and the tangent cylinder is **not** trivially produced by ordinary instantaneous tides.\n\nSo, stripped of interpretation, the calculations currently say:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{array}{l}\n1.\\ \\text{A natural spin/orbit worldtube-curvature crossover exists.}\\\\\n2.\\ \\text{Earth and Mars uniquely put it deeply inside substantial liquid interiors.}\\\\\n3.\\ \\text{Earth puts it unexpectedly near its inner-core tangent cylinder.}\\\\\n4.\\ \\text{Venus and the giant planets occupy very different limiting regimes.}\\\\\n5.\\ \\text{Ordinary tides only weakly perturb the Earth crossover.}\\\\\n6.\\ \\text{The terrestrial flip, if there is one, is not ordinary rigid-body tumbling.}\\\\\n7.\\ \\text{The remaining place to look is rotating-fluid / partially decoupled worldtube dynamics.}\n\\end{array}}\n\\]\n\nAnd your “Strong Gravity as something like macroscopic entanglement” idea can remain outside that calculation for now. If a history-dependent braid interaction exists, we would eventually expect it to modify the bound-system dynamics in a way that an instantaneous curvature field does not. But the useful thing is that we already have a baseline geometry against which any such residual would have to show itself.\n\nThe next hard calculation, I think, is therefore exactly the fluid-gyro problem: take the simplest known rotating-fluid instability that gives large orientation/vorticity reorganizations, radialize it, and see how the \\(\\kappa_s\\sim\\kappa_o\\) crossover enters the equations—if it enters at all."
          ]

The inner-core growth rate is uncertain and not constant, and Earth's spin evolution is also irregular.\n\nBut it suggests a precise possible relationship:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{phase-boundary migration and worldtube-curvature migration occur on comparable secular rates.}\n}\n\\]\n\nIf melting/freezing is partly the material resolution of bending-energy dissipation, that is exactly the kind of relationship we would expect to have to explain.\n\nIt also tells us something against the simplest “overdue” picture. The mean \\(106\\)-km separation between \\(r_*\\) and the present inner-core tangent cylinder evolves on roughly \\(10^8\\)-year scales, not \\(10^5\\)-year scales. If the reversal connection is real, individual reversals cannot simply be “the slowly moving mean crossover finally reaches the ICB.”\n\nInstead, we'd have:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{slow secular background}}\n\\]\n\nfrom spin evolution and inner-core growth,\n\nplus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{large orbital modulation}}\n\\]\n\nfrom eccentricity,\n\nplus fluid dynamics on much shorter timescales.\n\nThat is a much more plausible architecture for irregular threshold crossings.\n\nAnd now Venus.\n\nThe blind equation gives a very clean result. Ask what Venus's rotation period would have to be for the crossover merely to reach the planetary surface:\n\n\\[\nT_{\\rm crit}\n=\nT_{\\rm orb}\\sqrt{\\frac{R_V}{a_V}}.\n\\]\n\nUsing standard Venus values,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{T_{\\rm crit}\\approx1.68\\ {\\rm Earth\\ days}}\n\\]\n\nor about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{40.3\\ {\\rm h}}.\n\\]\n\nBut Venus presently rotates in about 243 Earth days retrograde. NASA gives roughly 243 days for the solid planet and about four days for the upper cloud circulation. citeturn438977search39\n\nSo its solid-body crossover is not just outside Venus. It is wildly outside:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{r_*}{R_V}\\approx2.09\\times10^4.\n\\]\n\nNow ask a more revealing blind question: what spin period would put Venus into the present Earth/Mars geometric class,\n\n\\[\nr_*/R\\sim0.15-0.18?\n\\]\n\nThe answer is only about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{16-17\\ {\\rm hours}}.\n\\]\n\nSo if Venus ever possessed an ordinary fast primordial spin of that general scale and subsequently evolved toward its present extraordinarily slow retrograde state, the crossover surface would have swept:\n\n\\[\n\\text{deep interior}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{mantle}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{surface}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{far outside the planet}.\n\\]\n\nThat conclusion doesn't require us to decide *why* Venus spun down.\n\nUnder the bending-energy/phase-change hypothesis, however, it gives a very strong implication: Venus should carry a dramatically different thermal/structural history from Earth precisely because its worldtube-curvature crossover has migrated completely out of the material body.\n\nAnd its atmosphere gives another control. A four-day rotation field gives roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{r_*/R_V\\sim5.7}.\n\\]\n\nStill outside—but vastly closer than the solid planet's \\(2\\times10^4\\).\n\nSo the solid Venus and its superrotating atmosphere occupy radically different locations in the same geometry while sharing the same planet.\n\nThat is almost tailor-made for the solid/liquid/gas test.\n\nOne caution on “melting = bending-energy dissipation”: equality\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_s=\\kappa_o\n\\]\n\ndoesn't automatically mean maximum heating. Standard elastic/viscous dissipation depends on strain and strain-rate invariants, not just equality of two curvature magnitudes. So the next proper calculation is to take the time-dependent combined curvature field and calculate its **rate of deformation** across the crossover region.\n\nBut the blind results already give us three targets that we did not select from magnetic or thermal data:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne_{\\rm crit,\\oplus}\\approx0.0445,\n\\qquad\n\\dot r_{*,\\oplus}\\approx0.60\\ {\\rm mm/yr},\n\\qquad\nT_{\\rm spin,V}^{(r_*=R)}\\approx40.3\\ {\\rm h}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThose are now predictions/retrodiction targets we can interrogate rather than knobs we chose to make the story work."

            "If by “full planetary resurfacing” you mean a geologically discrete episode in which essentially the entire established surface is reset, then among the eight planets the answer is basically:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\textbf{one: Venus.}}\n\\]\n\nVenus is the canonical case. Its sparse, nearly randomly distributed impact craters and broadly young surface led to the long-standing inference that most of the planet was resurfaced roughly \\(300\\)–\\(750\\) million years ago, possibly in a relatively abrupt global volcanic/tectonic episode. citeturn384435search0turn384435search1\n\nAnd none of the other rocky planets has an equivalent strongly suspected recent global reset:\n\n- **Earth:** essentially the whole crust gets recycled over geological time through plate tectonics, volcanism, erosion, etc., but that's continuous/patchwork recycling, not a Venus-style synchronous planetary resurfacing event.\n- **Mars:** huge regional volcanic and sedimentary resurfacing, and perhaps episodes with global consequences, but substantial ancient terrain survives. No comparable whole-surface reset.\n- **Mercury:** likewise, ancient terrains plus regional volcanic resurfacing, not a young globally reset surface.\n- **Jupiter/Saturn/Uranus/Neptune:** no persistent solid surface in the relevant sense.\n\nThere is an important modern caveat, though. The **single catastrophic Venus event is no longer something I'd call established**. Current Venus literature treats it as an active controversy: models range from catastrophic/episodic global resurfacing to spatially distributed resurfacing over an extended interval. A recent NASA review goes further and says the crater evidence does *not* favor a single catastrophic event during Venus's latest geological era. citeturn384435search2turn384435search30\n\nSo the particularly interesting statement for us is actually:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Venus is the only planet for which near-global resurfacing is a major live geological hypothesis.}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd that is rather conspicuous given what we just calculated.\n\nEarth/Mars:\n\n\\[\nr_*<R\n\\]\n\nwith the crossover embedded in their interiors.\n\nPresent Venus:\n\n\\[\nr_*/R\\sim2.1\\times10^4,\n\\]\n\nso the crossover is catastrophically far outside the solid planet.\n\nBut if Venus once rotated on a roughly terrestrial timescale, our blind calculation says \\(r_*\\) would have swept outward **through the entire planet** as Venus spun down.\n\nThat gives us a very sharp next question: **at what Venus rotation periods would \\(r_*\\) have crossed plausible core, mantle, lithosphere, and surface radii—and how long would it take to sweep through each under plausible Venus spin-evolution histories?**\n\nIf the resurfacing epoch falls anywhere near one of those crossings without us tuning for it, that becomes considerably more interesting. memcite"

Here’s the thing I should have gone straight to: if resurfacing follows the outward sweep of the crossover through Venusian material, the geometry predicts a strongly accelerating, apparently catastrophic final resurfacing phase.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nx\\equiv \\frac{r_*}{R_V}.\n\\]\n\nAs Venus spins down,\n\n\\[\nr_*\\propto T_s^2.\n\\]\n\nWhen the crossover cylinder intersects the spherical surface, its cylindrical radius is\n\n\\[\nr_*=R_V\\sin\\theta\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\theta\\) is colatitude. As \\(r_*\\) expands from the rotation axis to \\(R_V\\), it sweeps the surface from the poles toward the equator.\n\nThe fraction of the planetary surface that has been swept is just spherical geometry:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf=1-\\sqrt{1-x^2}\n}\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nx=\\left(\\frac{T_s}{T_{\\rm crit}}\\right)^2,\n\\qquad\nT_{\\rm crit}\\approx40.33\\ {\\rm h}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf(T_s)=\n1-\\sqrt{\n1-\\left(\\frac{T_s}{40.33\\ {\\rm h}}\\right)^4\n}\n}.\n\\]\n\nThat is already the blind resurfacing curve.\n\nAnd it is very nonlinear.\n\n| Surface swept | Venus day length |\n|---:|---:|\n| 10% | 26.63 h |\n| 25% | 32.80 h |\n| 50% | 37.53 h |\n| 75% | 39.68 h |\n| 90% | 40.229 h |\n| 95% | 40.305 h |\n| 99% | 40.3290 h |\n| 100% | 40.330 h |\n\nLook at the bottom of that table.\n\nThe first half of the planet requires Venus's day to change by nearly eleven hours:\n\n\\[\n26.6\\rightarrow37.5\\ {\\rm h}.\n\\]\n\nBut the final half occurs during only\n\n\\[\n37.53\\rightarrow40.33\\ {\\rm h}.\n\\]\n\nThe final 25%:\n\n\\[\n39.68\\rightarrow40.33\\ {\\rm h}.\n\\]\n\nThe final 10%:\n\n\\[\n40.229\\rightarrow40.330\\ {\\rm h},\n\\]\n\nonly about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{6.1\\ {\\rm minutes}}\n\\]\n\nof additional spin-period evolution.\n\nAnd the final 1% requires only about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{3.6\\ {\\rm seconds}}\n\\]\n\nof change in Venus's day length.\n\nThat does **not** mean the final 1% resurfaces in seconds. It means that if spin-down is gradual, an extraordinarily small amount of further spin evolution sweeps a large fraction of the remaining surface.\n\nThat is the interesting prediction.\n\nNow put a timescale on it without looking at resurfacing chronology.\n\nDefine the local spin-evolution timescale\n\n\\[\n\\tau_s\\equiv\n\\left|\\frac{d\\ln T_s}{dt}\\right|^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nThen because \\(r_*\\propto T_s^2\\),\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\dot r_*}{r_*}=\\frac{2}{\\tau_s}.\n\\]\n\nAt the Venus surface,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\dot r_*\n=\n\\frac{2R_V}{\\tau_s}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor a nominal\n\n\\[\n\\tau_s=1\\ {\\rm Gyr},\n\\]\n\nthe crossover moves outward at about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{12.1\\ {\\rm km/Myr}}.\n\\]\n\nBut the area swept per radial kilometre blows up geometrically as the cylinder approaches the equator. I did the calculation we actually needed, and it gives one important negative result followed by a much more interesting conditional positive one.\n\nFirst, the bare spin/orbit crossover is not automatically a dissipation surface in standard continuum mechanics.\n\nFor rigid orbital translation plus rigid spin,\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf u(\\mathbf x,t)\n=\n\\mathbf V_{\\rm orb}(t)+\\boldsymbol\\Omega\\times\\mathbf x.\n\\]\n\nThe strain-rate tensor is\n\n\\[\nD_{ij}\n=\n\\frac12\n\\left(\n\\partial_i u_j+\\partial_j u_i\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nTranslation contributes no gradient, and rigid rotation contributes an antisymmetric gradient. Therefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{D_{ij}=0}.\n\\]\n\nThe ordinary viscous dissipation density,\n\n\\[\n\\Phi=2\\eta D_{ij}D_{ij},\n\\]\n\nis consequently\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Phi=0}.\n\\]\n\nSo merely having\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_{\\rm spin}=\\kappa_{\\rm orbit}\n\\]\n\ndoes not make things heat up. That's a useful kill shot against the naive version of the melting idea.\n\nLikewise, if I temporarily treat curvature as ordinary elastic bending, \\(U\\propto\\kappa^2\\), equality of two curvatures produces no generic energy maximum. Depending on their relative directions it can even produce a minimum.\n\nSo if the “wrung rope” idea has teeth, the relevant ordinary mathematical objects are going to be **twist, shear, changing preferred orientation, and hysteretic deformation**, not merely curvature equality.\n\nNow the interesting part.\n\nThere is a minimal back-of-envelope version of the hypothesis that adds no mysterious energy source:\n\n> The energy available for a crossover-driven restructuring is the planet's ordinary lost rotational kinetic energy, and the moving crossover localizes some fraction of that dissipation into the material it sweeps.\n\nThat is an assumption, not something we've derived. But once we make it, the rest is calculable.\n\nFor Venus, taking\n\n\\[\nC\\simeq0.337MR^2\\simeq6.0\\times10^{37}\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^2},\n\\]\n\nthe rotational energy is\n\n\\[\nE_{\\rm rot}=\\frac12C\\Omega^2.\n\\]\n\nAt the spin period where our crossover reaches the surface,\n\n\\[\nT_c\\simeq40.33\\ {\\rm h},\n\\]\n\nVenus carries approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{E_{\\rm rot}\\simeq5.63\\times10^{28}\\ {\\rm J}}.\n\\]\n\nIts current 243-day spin contains essentially none of that by comparison. Thus the rotational-energy decrease from the \\(40.3\\)-hour state to today's state is about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta E\\simeq5.6\\times10^{28}\\ {\\rm J}}.\n\\]\n\nIf Venus came from a 30-hour spin,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta E\\sim1.0\\times10^{29}\\ {\\rm J},\n\\]\n\nand from a 16-hour spin,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta E\\sim3.6\\times10^{29}\\ {\\rm J}.\n\\]\n\nThose are enormous geological energy budgets.\n\nFor scale, taking roughly\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm melt}\\sim10^6\\ {\\rm J\\,kg^{-1}}\n\\]\n\nto heat and melt silicate and \\(\\rho\\sim3000\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^{-3}}\\), \\(5.6\\times10^{28}\\) J corresponds, if all of it went into melting, to roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{40\\ {\\rm km}}\n\\]\n\nof globally averaged rock.\n\nThat's an upper bound, emphatically—not a prediction that Venus melted 40 km deep.\n\nNow do the geometry of the sweep.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nx=\\frac{r_*}{R}\n=\n\\left(\\frac{T}{T_c}\\right)^2.\n\\]\n\nThe fraction of the spherical surface reached by an expanding coaxial cylinder is\n\n\\[\nf_A=1-\\sqrt{1-x^2}.\n\\]\n\nBut the fraction of planetary volume inside that cylinder is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf_V\n=\n1-(1-x^2)^{3/2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThose two functions behave very differently near the surface.\n\nIn fact,\n\n\\[\n1-f_V=(1-f_A)^3.\n\\]\n\nThat's the interesting geometrical lever.\n\nIf 90% of the surface has been swept, only\n\n\\[\n(0.10)^3=0.001\n\\]\n\nof the planetary volume remains outside the crossover.\n\nAt 99% surface coverage,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1-f_V=10^{-6}}.\n\\]\n\nThe last one percent of surface corresponds to only one millionth of the planet's volume in this simple cylindrical sweep geometry.\n\nNow distribute the rotational energy lost during each increment of spin-down into the newly swept volume. The mean deposited specific energy in the final remaining volume rises very sharply.\n\nUsing the Venus numbers:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{array}{c|c}\n\\text{surface already swept} & \n\\text{mean energy available in remaining swept volume}\\\\\n\\hline\n90\\% & \\sim0.10\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}\\\\\n95\\% & \\sim0.20\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}\\\\\n98\\% & \\sim0.51\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}\\\\\n99\\% & \\boxed{\\sim1.01\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}}\\\\\n99.3\\% & \\sim1.44\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}\\\\\n99.5\\% & \\sim2.02\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}\n\\end{array}\n\\]\n\nThat caught my attention.\n\nUnder this very specific localization hypothesis, the final roughly one percent of the geometric sweep naturally reaches the order of magnitude required for wholesale silicate heating/melting.\n\nWe didn't insert a melting energy to make the geometry hit at 99%; I used the standard rough \\(1\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}\\) afterward as the comparison.\n\nNow the timescale.\n\nDefine the local fractional spin-evolution timescale\n\n\\[\n\\tau_s=\\frac{T}{|\\dot T|}.\n\\]\n\nWith \\(r_*\\propto T^2\\), the time remaining after fraction \\(f_A\\) of the surface has been swept is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta t\n=\n-\\frac{\\tau_s}{4}\n\\ln(2f_A-f_A^2).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the final 1%,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta t_{99\\rightarrow100}\n\\simeq2.5\\times10^{-5}\\tau_s.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is the useful prediction because we don't have to choose Venus's ancient spin-down rate yet.\n\nIf the relevant spin-evolution timescale was\n\n\\[\n\\tau_s=0.1\\ {\\rm Gyr},\n\\]\n\nthe terminal phase lasts about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2,500\\ {\\rm yr}}.\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\tau_s=1\\ {\\rm Gyr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{25,000\\ {\\rm yr}}.\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\tau_s=10\\ {\\rm Gyr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{250,000\\ {\\rm yr}}.\n\\]\n\nEven an extremely slow secular spin evolution therefore turns into a comparatively abrupt geological event at the end of the cylindrical sweep.\n\nThe corresponding geometrical surface-sweep rate, taking \\(\\tau_s=1\\) Gyr merely as a normalization, is approximately:\n\n\\[\n90\\%:\\quad9\\ {\\rm km^2/yr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n95\\%:\\quad18\\ {\\rm km^2/yr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n99\\%:\\quad\\boxed{92\\ {\\rm km^2/yr}},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n99.9\\%:\\quad\\boxed{920\\ {\\rm km^2/yr}}.\n\\]\n\nMultiply those rates by \\(1\\,{\\rm Gyr}/\\tau_s\\) for any other spin-evolution timescale.\n\nSo the bounded calculation says something remarkably specific:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{slow rotational evolution can map into a very rapid terminal geological sweep.}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd if—big **if**—lost rotational energy preferentially dissipates in material undergoing that sweep, the final-stage energy density becomes large enough to enter the silicate-melting regime.\n\nThat's considerably stronger than where we were two turns ago.\n\nBut it also tells us exactly what must be true for your “planets are wrung ropes” picture to work. The crossover itself isn't enough. There has to be a mechanism whereby changing **twist/shear configuration** concentrates ordinary mechanical energy near that migrating geometric structure.\n\nWhich means I would now switch mathematical objects.\n\nNot another curvature scalar.\n\nFor a wrung rope, the standard language is Kirchhoff/Cosserat rod mechanics: a material-frame twist vector, bending strains, torsional strain energy, and—in fluid regions—the corresponding shear/vorticity dynamics and viscous dissipation. If the planetary worldtube really behaves more like a wound bundle than a spinning ball, that's where it should announce itself mathematically.\n\nAnd that would indeed eventually make questions of the Yellowstone/Deccan-Traps type calculable in principle: not “is Yellowstone scary?”, but whether Earth's present mapped twist/dissipation geometry predicts spatially concentrated unloading events, where they migrate, and on what timescale.\n\nWe should not look at Yellowstone yet.\n\nFirst I want to calculate the **torsional** version of the Venus sweep blind. That is the wrung-rope test."

            "I calculated the actual torsional/Cosserat version, and it gives us a useful correction.\n\nThe bare “wrung rope” torsion does not by itself produce catastrophic resurfacing. The dramatic terminal blow-up in the previous calculation came from assuming that essentially all of the planet’s lost rotational energy was being localized into the shrinking region swept last. Ordinary torsional mechanics does not do that automatically.\n\nIn the radialized picture, the standard material-frame twist density is\n\n\\[\nq_s=\\frac{\\omega}{c},\n\\]\n\nwith orbital frame winding\n\n\\[\nq_o=\\frac{n}{c}.\n\\]\n\nAt the Venus surface-crossing state,\n\n\\[\nT_s\\simeq40.33\\ {\\rm h},\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\nq_s\\simeq1.44\\times10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m^{-1}},\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\nq_o\\simeq1.08\\times10^{-15}\\ {\\rm m^{-1}}.\n\\]\n\nSo\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac{q_s}{q_o}\\simeq134.}\n\\]\n\nThat's important. Our crossover at \\(r_*=R_V\\) is not a torsion-equality condition. It comes from\n\n\\[\n\\omega^2R_V=n^2a,\n\\]\n\nan equality of centripetal/worldline-curvature scales. The twist rates themselves are nowhere near equal there.\n\nNow treat Venus literally as an elastic twisted continuum. The standard torsional shear strain at cylindrical radius \\(r_\\perp\\) would be\n\n\\[\n\\gamma=r_\\perp q_s\n=\\frac{r_\\perp\\omega}{c}.\n\\]\n\nAt the surface at \\(40.33\\) h,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\gamma_{\\max}\\simeq8.74\\times10^{-7}}.\n\\]\n\nTaking a representative rocky shear modulus\n\n\\[\n\\mu\\simeq60\\ {\\rm GPa},\n\\]\n\nthe elastic torsional energy density is only\n\n\\[\nu_\\tau=\\frac12\\mu\\gamma^2\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{u_{\\tau,\\max}\\simeq2.3\\times10^{-2}\\ {\\rm J\\,m^{-3}}.}\n\\]\n\nCompare that with roughly\n\n\\[\n\\sim 10^9\\!-\\!10^{10}\\ {\\rm J\\,m^{-3}}\n\\]\n\nto heat and melt silicate.\n\nWe're short by roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{10^{11}}\n\\]\n\nin energy density.\n\nIntegrated over a uniform Venus-sized sphere,\n\n\\[\nE_\\tau\n=\n\\frac{\\mu VR^2\\omega^2}{5c^2}\n\\]\n\ngives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{E_\\tau\\simeq8.5\\times10^{18}\\ {\\rm J}.}\n\\]\n\nBut Venus's ordinary rotational kinetic energy at that spin state is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{E_{\\rm rot}\\simeq5.6\\times10^{28}\\ {\\rm J}.}\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{E_\\tau}{E_{\\rm rot}}\n\\simeq1.5\\times10^{-10}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf you converted that literal elastic worldtube-twist energy completely into melting, you'd globally melt only a few micrometres of rock.\n\nSo:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{literal elastic torsion of the radialized material worldtube is not the resurfacing energy source.}}\n\\]\n\nThat's a strong negative result.\n\nThere's another useful result. Because torsional energy density scales as \\(r_\\perp^2\\), we can calculate how much of the twist energy lies inside our expanding crossover cylinder.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nx=\\frac{r_*}{R}.\n\\]\n\nFor a uniform sphere, the fraction of torsional energy inside that cylinder is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_\\tau(x)\n=\n1-\\frac52(1-x^2)^{3/2}\n+\\frac32(1-x^2)^{5/2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nRecall that the surface fraction swept is\n\n\\[\nf=1-\\sqrt{1-x^2}.\n\\]\n\nSet\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon=1-f.\n\\]\n\nThen the torsional energy remaining outside the cylinder is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n1-F_\\tau\n=\n\\frac12\\epsilon^3(5-3\\epsilon^2).\n}\n\\]\n\nBut the remaining volume fraction is simply\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon^3.\n\\]\n\nTherefore the mean torsional energy density in the last unswept region, relative to the planetary mean, tends only to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac52}\n\\]\n\nas the sweep approaches completion.\n\nNo divergence.\n\nSo the earlier terminal-catastrophe result is not intrinsic to ordinary torsional geometry. We had implicitly introduced a strong localization assumption.\n\nThat's exactly the sort of thing these blind calculations are supposed to catch.\n\nHowever, there is still a real large energy reservoir available: ordinary rotational energy lost during despinning. So I then calculated the standard tidal despinning clock around the \\(40\\)-hour Venus state.\n\nVenus's measured degree-two Love number is about\n\n\\[\nk_2=0.295\\pm0.066,\n\\]\n\nand published Venus dissipation estimates commonly put \\(Q\\) roughly in the \\(20\\)–\\(100\\) range, although \\(Q\\) remains poorly constrained. citeturn318754search1turn318754search5\n\nUsing the basic constant-\\(Q\\) equilibrium-tide torque,\n\n\\[\nN\\simeq\n\\frac32\\frac{k_2}{Q}\n\\frac{GM_\\odot^2R^5}{a^6},\n\\]\n\nat \\(T_s=40.33\\) h I get\n\n\\[\nN\\simeq\n5.9\\times10^{15}\n\\text{ to }\n3.0\\times10^{16}\\ {\\rm N\\,m}.\n\\]\n\nThat corresponds to a local despinning timescale\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau_s=\\frac{\\omega}{|\\dot\\omega|}\n\\simeq2.8-14\\ {\\rm Gyr}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis simple equilibrium-tide model is only an approximation for Venus; atmospheric tides, frequency-dependent rheology, and the choice of tidal model matter substantially. Published Venus evolution work explicitly warns about that. citeturn318754search3\n\nBut it's a good blind normalization.\n\nNow combine that standard torque with our purely geometric cylindrical sweep. The time from a given swept surface fraction to the crossover reaching the equator comes out approximately:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{array}{c|c}\n\\text{surface already crossed} & \\text{time remaining}\\\\\n\\hline\n50\\% & 0.21-1.04\\ {\\rm Gyr}\\\\\n90\\% & 7.0-35\\ {\\rm Myr}\\\\\n95\\% & 1.75-8.7\\ {\\rm Myr}\\\\\n99\\% & 70-349\\ {\\rm kyr}\\\\\n99.5\\% & 17-87\\ {\\rm kyr}\\\\\n99.9\\% & 0.7-3.5\\ {\\rm kyr}\n\\end{array}\n\\]\n\nThat result survives.\n\nSo Venus still has a very sharp geometric terminal sweep even under perfectly ordinary tidal despinning. What does **not** survive is the claim that ordinary torsional elasticity automatically dumps enough energy into that sweep to melt the planet.\n\nThere is one conditional result worth keeping. Suppose—not derive, just test—that lost rotational energy gets preferentially dissipated in the region whose worldtube configuration is actively reorganizing as the crossover passes.\n\nThen, because the remaining geometric volume shrinks as\n\n\\[\n(1-f)^3,\n\\]\n\nwhile rotational energy continues to be lost, the specific available energy rises very rapidly.\n\nUsing an outer-rock density around \\(3300\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^{-3}}\\), the energy available between a given surface fraction and completion would be approximately:\n\n\\[\n90\\%:\\quad0.09\\ {\\rm MJ/kg},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n95\\%:\\quad0.18\\ {\\rm MJ/kg},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n99\\%:\\quad0.92\\ {\\rm MJ/kg},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n99.5\\%:\\quad1.84\\ {\\rm MJ/kg},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n99.9\\%:\\quad9.2\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}.\n\\]\n\nA rough heat-plus-melt requirement of \\(1\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}\\) is crossed at about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{f\\simeq99.08\\%.}\n\\]\n\nUnder the \\(Q=20\\)–\\(100\\) tidal normalization, that occurs roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{59-294\\ {\\rm kyr}}\n\\]\n\nbefore the crossover reaches the equator.\n\nThat is a remarkable conditional timescale.\n\nBut notice what it actually predicts spatially: without some global failure/cascade mechanism, the directly catastrophic part should be concentrated into the final roughly \\(1\\%\\) equatorial surface band, not automatically the entire planet.\n\nSo our calculation has divided the “wrung rope” idea into two very different versions:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{ordinary elastic twist}\n\\quad\\Rightarrow\\quad\n\\text{far too little energy}\n}\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{history-dependent redistribution of ordinary rotational energy}\n\\quad\\Rightarrow\\quad\n\\text{potentially geological-scale energy on }10^4\\!-\\!10^5\\text{ yr terminal timescales}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe second is the interesting one—but the localization/hysteresis is exactly what still needs to fall out of the geometry rather than be assumed.\n\nAnd this already restrains the Yellowstone speculation. Earth's present crossover is at only\n\n\\[\nr_*/R_\\oplus\\simeq0.175.\n\\]\n\nIt is deep inside the planet, nowhere near the surface-terminal regime Venus would have crossed. So this particular Venus geometry does **not** immediately say “Yellowstone is headed for a Deccan event.”\n\nIf a Deccan/Yellowstone connection exists in this picture, it has to come through the way deep twist/vorticity redistribution couples upward through the mantle—not simply from \\(r_*\\) reaching the lithosphere.\n\nThat is the calculation I'd do next: take Earth's current deep crossover and ask whether standard viscoelastic/torsional transport from that cylindrical region naturally produces preferred mantle pathways, timescales, and surface concentrations. That would give us something we can compare blindly to large igneous provinces and hotspots afterward. memcite"
