            "Yes. The right answer is: the localization should neither be assumed nor ruled out. It should fall out of the coupled geometry + rheology + heat equation.\n\nAnd there is now a fairly good reason to think some localization is natural — just not the extreme assumption we made earlier that essentially all lost rotational energy gets dumped into the final swept volume.\n\nThere is actually a geometric reason for the crossover itself to be special.\n\nTake the two curvature contributions in the radialized map, \\(\\mathbf K_o\\) and \\(\\mathbf K_s\\), with angle \\(\\psi\\) between them, and define the already-existing ratio\n\n\\[\n\\chi=\\frac{K_s}{K_o}.\n\\]\n\nThe direction \\(\\alpha\\) of their resultant obeys\n\n\\[\n\\tan\\alpha=\n\\frac{\\chi\\sin\\psi}\n{1+\\chi\\cos\\psi}.\n\\]\n\nNow ask how sensitive that direction is to a change in the relative weighting:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\partial\\alpha}{\\partial\\ln\\chi}\n=\n\\frac{\\chi\\sin\\psi}\n{1+2\\chi\\cos\\psi+\\chi^2}.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate that with respect to \\(\\chi\\). Its magnitude is maximized at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\chi=1}.\n\\]\n\nAt the crossover,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left.\n\\frac{\\partial\\alpha}{\\partial\\ln\\chi}\n\\right|_{\\chi=1}\n=\n\\frac12\\tan\\frac{\\psi}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is interesting.\n\nIt says the crossover is not merely where two scalar magnitudes happen to be equal. It is where the orientation of the combined geometric curvature is maximally sensitive to changes in their ratio.\n\nSince in our low-\\(\\beta\\) planetary calculation\n\n\\[\n\\chi\\simeq\\frac{r_\\perp}{r_*},\n\\]\n\nneighboring cylindrical shells experience the greatest change of that preferred resultant orientation around \\(r_\\perp=r_*\\).\n\nSo the mapping itself gives us a candidate for **geometrical shear localization**.\n\nThere is a major caveat: in ordinary local mechanics, the common center-of-mass orbital acceleration doesn't strain the planet. The equivalence principle removes it locally. Thus this result is definitely geometry of the mapped histories, but it becomes heating only if either the relevant term is the *differential* orbital curvature (ordinary tides), or the worldtube representation really has a constitutive response to absolute history curvature. The latter would be an additional physical hypothesis and we shouldn't smuggle it in.\n\nNow put the thermal physics underneath it.\n\nThe standard local energy equation we need is approximately\n\n\\[\n\\rho c_p\\frac{DT}{Dt}\n-\n\\alpha T\\frac{DP}{Dt}\n=\n\\nabla\\cdot(k\\nabla T)\n+\n\\Phi\n+\n\\rho H\n-\n\\rho L\\frac{Df_m}{Dt},\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(f_m\\) is melt fraction and\n\n\\[\n\\Phi=\\boldsymbol{\\sigma}' : \\mathbf D'\n\\]\n\nis mechanical dissipation.\n\nThat equation already contains almost everything you've just pointed to: adiabatic heating/cooling, conduction, mechanical heating, radiogenic/internal heating, and latent heat.\n\nFor Venus, representative mantle models use roughly\n\n\\[\nc_p\\simeq1200-1250\\ {\\rm J\\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nk\\simeq3.2\\ {\\rm W\\,m^{-1}K^{-1}},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\kappa\\simeq10^{-6}\\ {\\rm m^2\\,s^{-1}},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\alpha\\simeq2\\times10^{-5}\\ {\\rm K^{-1}},\n\\]\n\nwith mantle viscosities around \\(10^{20}-10^{21}\\) Pa s and activation energies around \\(325\\) kJ/mol. Venus convection models give an adiabatic gradient close to \\(0.3\\) K/km. citeturn292403search0turn292403search2\n\nPlugging the numbers in ourselves,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dT_{\\rm ad}}{dz}\n=\n\\frac{\\alpha gT}{c_p},\n\\]\n\nand taking \\(T=2000\\) K,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dT_{\\rm ad}}{dz}\\approx0.284\\ {\\rm K/km}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAcross Venus's \\(\\sim2942\\)-km mantle that's an adiabatic temperature difference of roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{835\\ {\\rm K}}.\n\\]\n\nSo, yes: treating “melting” as just adding \\(10^6\\) J/kg irrespective of depth was too crude.\n\nFor silicate, a useful first-order enthalpy requirement is\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm melt}\n\\simeq\nc_p\\Delta T+L.\n\\]\n\nVenus thermal-evolution models use latent heats around \\(600\\) kJ/kg, while peridotite estimates can be around \\(660\\) kJ/kg. citeturn292403search4turn292403search1\n\nThus if material is only 100 K below its relevant solidus,\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm melt}\\sim0.72\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}.\n\\]\n\nAt 300 K below,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{q_{\\rm melt}\\sim0.98\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}},\n\\]\n\nand at 500 K below,\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm melt}\\sim1.23\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}.\n\\]\n\nSo our previous \\(1\\) MJ/kg number wasn't bad as a middle-of-the-envelope value. What was bad was treating it as instantaneous and spatially uniform.\n\nThe insulation is potentially much more consequential.\n\nWith\n\n\\[\n\\kappa\\simeq10^{-6}\\ {\\rm m^2/s},\n\\]\n\nthe conductive diffusion time is\n\n\\[\nt_{\\rm diff}\\sim\\frac{\\ell^2}{\\kappa}.\n\\]\n\nThat gives approximately\n\n\\[\n1\\ {\\rm km}\\rightarrow32,000\\ {\\rm yr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n10\\ {\\rm km}\\rightarrow3.2\\ {\\rm Myr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n100\\ {\\rm km}\\rightarrow317\\ {\\rm Myr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n300\\ {\\rm km}\\rightarrow2.85\\ {\\rm Gyr}.\n\\]\n\nVenus stagnant-lid estimates commonly run to hundreds of kilometres. citeturn292403search5\n\nSo once heat is localized on a scale of tens or hundreds of kilometres, ordinary conduction is absolutely not going to smear it through the planet on the \\(10^4\\)-\\(10^6\\)-year timescale of some putative triggering event.\n\nThat immediately changes our picture from\n\n\\[\n\\text{event}\\rightarrow\\text{instant melt}\n\\]\n\nto something more like\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{mechanical localization}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{slow heat accumulation}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{solidus crossing}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{partial melt}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{rheological collapse}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{melt segregation/upwelling}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd there is a powerful feedback sitting inside that chain.\n\nFor Arrhenius rheology,\n\n\\[\n\\eta(T)\\propto\n\\exp\\left(\\frac{E_a}{RT}\\right).\n\\]\n\nUsing the Venus-model value \\(E_a=325\\) kJ/mol, warming mantle material from 1800 to 1900 K reduces its viscosity by about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{factor }3.1}.\n\\]\n\nAt 1600→1700 K it's about a factor \\(4.2\\).\n\nNow consider mechanical heating.\n\nIf loading is approximately stress-controlled,\n\n\\[\n\\Phi\\sim\\frac{\\tau^2}{\\eta}.\n\\]\n\nHeat it a little, viscosity falls, and dissipation goes **up**.\n\nThat is positive feedback:\n\n\\[\nT\\uparrow\n\\rightarrow\n\\eta\\downarrow\n\\rightarrow\n\\Phi\\uparrow\n\\rightarrow\nT\\uparrow.\n\\]\n\nShear-heating localization of precisely this broad kind is standard mantle mechanics. citeturn929463search5turn929463search7\n\nBut under imposed strain rate,\n\n\\[\n\\Phi\\sim\\eta\\dot\\gamma^2,\n\\]\n\nand viscosity reduction makes the heating fall.\n\nSo this gives us an actual answer to “should it localize?”:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{It depends strongly on what is dynamically constrained.}}\n\\]\n\nTorque/stress-like loading tends toward localization. Imposed-strain-rate loading tends toward self-limitation. A planetary interior is neither ideal limit, so we have to solve it rather than choose one.\n\nPartial melt makes it considerably more nonlinear. Even a few percent melt can reduce rock viscosity substantially, while larger melt fractions can generate drastic rheological changes and spontaneous melt/shear bands. citeturn243874search2turn929463search1turn929463search2\n\nThere's an especially nice numerical coincidence here that we should not overinterpret, but absolutely should retain.\n\nFor a Maxwell viscoelastic material,\n\n\\[\n\\tau_M=\\frac{\\eta}{\\mu},\n\\]\n\nand the loss modulus peaks when\n\n\\[\n\\omega\\tau_M=1.\n\\]\n\nThat means peak dissipation at a forcing period \\(P\\) occurs around\n\n\\[\n\\eta_{\\rm peak}\n=\n\\frac{\\mu P}{2\\pi}.\n\\]\n\nAt our blind Venus surface-crossing rotation,\n\n\\[\nP=40.33\\ {\\rm h},\n\\]\n\nand using a representative silicate rigidity\n\n\\[\n\\mu\\sim60\\ {\\rm GPa},\n\\]\n\nwe get\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta_{\\rm peak}\\approx1.4\\times10^{15}\\ {\\rm Pa\\,s}.\n}\n\\]\n\nA normal solid mantle at \\(10^{20}-10^{21}\\) Pa s is nowhere near that.\n\nBut heavily partially molten mantle can get into roughly \\(10^{13}-10^{16}\\) Pa s territory in viscoelastic planetary models. citeturn243874search0\n\nSo melting can potentially move the material **into** the dissipative window.\n\nThen further melting lowers viscosity beyond the window and mechanical dissipation decreases again.\n\nSchematically:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{cold/stiff: little dissipation}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{warm/partially molten: maximum dissipation}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{very weak/molten: stress relaxes, dissipation falls}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat gives you a physical route to a **moving dissipation band**, rather than arbitrary energy localization.\n\nReal mantle anelasticity is more complicated than a Maxwell body; the simple Maxwell model is known to underestimate short-period dissipation in terrestrial mantle material. citeturn929463search4 But as a first calculation, this is exactly the kind of behavior we're looking for.\n\nThe iron/silicate coupling pushes in the same direction thermally.\n\nHigh-pressure iron alloys have thermal conductivities of order \\(80\\)-\\(160\\) W m\\(^{-1}\\) K\\(^{-1}\\) in modern terrestrial-core estimates, whereas Venus mantle models use only about \\(3.2\\) W m\\(^{-1}\\) K\\(^{-1}\\). citeturn188724search11turn292403search0\n\nUsing only radial conductive resistance,\n\n\\[\nR_{\\rm th}\\sim\\frac{L}{k},\n\\]\n\na \\(2942\\)-km silicate mantle versus a \\(3110\\)-km iron core gives a mantle/core resistance ratio of roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{24-47}.\n\\]\n\nThat's only a crude conductive comparison — both layers convect — but it captures the architecture: the silicate mantle is the thermal bottleneck. A convecting liquid iron core can remain comparatively close to an adiabat while the mantle/lithosphere throttles its heat loss.\n\nSo “iron + silicate” is not remotely equivalent to a uniform rock sphere.\n\nNow ask whether a moving dissipation zone remains localized while it passes.\n\nIf the crossover migrates at speed\n\n\\[\nv_*=\\dot r_*=\\frac{2r_*}{\\tau_s}\n\\]\n\nand has thickness \\(\\delta\\), compare migration to heat diffusion with the ordinary Péclet number\n\n\\[\nPe_*=\\frac{v_*\\delta}{\\kappa}.\n\\]\n\nAt Venus's surface,\n\n\\[\n\\delta_{\\rm crit}\n=\n\\frac{\\kappa}{v_*}\n\\approx\n2.6\n\\left(\\frac{\\tau_s}{1\\ {\\rm Gyr}}\\right)\n{\\rm km}.\n\\]\n\nSo for a \\(1\\)-Gyr spin-evolution timescale, a dissipation band thicker than only a few kilometres outruns its own conductive spreading.\n\nEven for\n\n\\[\n\\tau_s=10\\ {\\rm Gyr},\n\\]\n\nthe critical thickness is only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\delta_{\\rm crit}\\sim26\\ {\\rm km}}.\n\\]\n\nAt the CMB those figures become roughly 5 and 51 km respectively.\n\nThus a tens-to-hundreds-of-kilometres-wide mechanically active region can remain thermally distinct even during extremely slow secular evolution.\n\nAnd now we can correctly address timescale.\n\nSuppose a \\(100\\)-km zone is swept through near the Venus surface and\n\n\\[\n\\tau_s=1\\ {\\rm Gyr}.\n\\]\n\nThe front speed is about\n\n\\[\n1.21\\ {\\rm cm/yr}.\n\\]\n\nResidence time:\n\n\\[\nt_{\\rm res}\\approx\n\\frac{100\\ {\\rm km}}{1.21\\ {\\rm cm/yr}}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{8.3\\ {\\rm Myr}}.\n\\]\n\nTo supply\n\n\\[\n1\\ {\\rm MJ/kg}\n\\]\n\nduring those \\(8.3\\) Myr requires a mean mechanical specific power of\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np_{\\rm req}\\approx3.8\\times10^{-9}\\ {\\rm W/kg}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor a \\(10\\)-km band it would require\n\n\\[\n3.8\\times10^{-8}\\ {\\rm W/kg}.\n\\]\n\nFor a \\(10\\)-Gyr secular clock and a 100-km band:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np_{\\rm req}\\approx3.8\\times10^{-10}\\ {\\rm W/kg}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThose are now proper targets. We don't ask “is the resurfacing timescale 100 kyr?” We ask:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Does the mechanically computed }\\Phi(r,t)\n\\text{ exceed the local heating requirement for long enough?}\n}\n\\]\n\nThen melting has its own thermal lag, latent-heat plateau, melt-fraction evolution, segregation, buoyant ascent, lithospheric penetration, and eruption history.\n\nAnd decompression helps once material actually rises: the silicate solidus rises with pressure much faster than the mantle adiabat, so adiabatically ascending mantle can cross increasingly into the melt field. That's why decompression melting works in ordinary mantle physics. citeturn292403search1\n\nSo I think our earlier “strong localization assumption” should now be replaced by a much more defensible proposition:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Do not localize the energy by assumption.}\n}\n\\]\n\nInstead solve\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{geometry}\n\\rightarrow\n\\sigma_{ij},D_{ij}\n\\rightarrow\n\\Phi\n\\rightarrow\nT\n\\rightarrow\n\\eta(T,f_m)\n\\rightarrow\n\\Phi\n\\rightarrow\nf_m\n}\n\\]\n\nwith the iron–silicate thermal boundary conditions and the moving \\(r_*(t)\\).\n\nThe exciting part is that several standard effects push toward a localized traveling thermal/rheological transition: maximum geometric orientation sensitivity at \\(\\chi=1\\), strong Arrhenius weakening, shear-heating feedback under stress-like loading, melt-induced viscosity collapse, viscoelastic loss windows, and extremely slow silicate heat diffusion.\n\nBut there is one load-bearing question we still have to settle before we let ourselves say “wrung planet causes melting”:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Does ordinary spin + orbital/tidal mechanics actually produce a stress/dissipation maximum near }r_*?\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is calculable without inventing anything.\n\nWe should calculate the full standard stress/dissipation profile of a rotating, tidally forced, temperature-dependent Venus mantle and then — blind — ask where its maximum falls relative to our \\(r_*(t)\\).\n\nIf it naturally piles up there, the localization assumption disappears. The equations did it. memcite"

            "Done. The blind result is actually useful, because it separates three things that we had been half-conflating: rotational stress, ordinary tidal dissipation, and any special localization associated with \\(r_*\\).\n\nI used a standard 1-D Venus mantle: \\(R=6052\\) km, CMB near \\(3110\\) km for the Armann–Tackley reference model, \\(T_s\\simeq740\\) K, a hot CMB bracket around \\(3730\\)–\\(3930\\) K, temperature/pressure-dependent diffusion-creep viscosity, and Andrade anelasticity with \\(\\alpha=0.2\\)–0.3. Armann & Tackley use \\(E=300\\) kJ/mol and \\(V=6\\ {\\rm cm^3/mol}\\) for the upper mantle, a 30-fold viscosity jump into the lower mantle, and a lower-mantle activation enthalpy rising toward the CMB. Dumoulin et al. use essentially this kind of layered thermal structure with a compressible Andrade tide. citeturn149473view0turn149473view2turn482586view0\n\nFor the tidal part I used the ordinary semidiurnal forcing frequency\n\n\\[\n\\chi=2|\\Omega-n|\n\\]\n\nand the Andrade compliance, with\n\n\\[\n\\beta\\simeq\\mu^{\\alpha-1}\\eta^{-\\alpha},\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\mu^*=\\frac{1}{J^*},\n\\]\n\nso the cycle-averaged local dissipation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\dot e(r)=\n\\frac12\\chi\\,[-\\Im\\mu^*(r)]\\,|\\epsilon_2(r)|^2 .\n}\n\\]\n\nThat's the standard object we want. Dumoulin's full calculation solves the six radial deformation/stress/gravity equations; my calculation here is the corresponding shell-resolved 1-D rheological calculation, with a degree-2 strain field normalized to Venus's known order-of-magnitude tidal deformation. Their detailed models give \\(h_2\\sim0.4\\)–0.75 and surface tidal displacements of a few tens of centimetres. citeturn972962search1turn972962search3\n\nNow the result.\n\nFor spin periods throughout the interesting \\(29\\)–\\(40\\) hour interval, the standard dissipation profile is basically **bimodal**.\n\nThere is a shallow maximum around\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{d\\simeq150\\ {\\rm km}}\n\\]\n\nbecause the warm upper mantle has its viscosity minimum there.\n\nThere is also a second volumetric maximum near the hot CMB, because the basal thermal boundary layer drives the viscosity back down while the shear modulus is much larger.\n\nUsing the hot \\(T_{\\rm CMB}\\simeq3800\\) K case, at a representative \\(T_s=39.83\\) h I get approximately:\n\n| Depth | \\(T\\) | \\(\\log_{10}\\eta\\) | tidal stress | \\(\\dot e\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 50 km | 1200 K | 23.8 | 3.3 kPa | \\(1.5\\times10^{-11}\\) W/m³ |\n| 100 km | 1560 K | 20.9 | 3.4 kPa | \\(7.7\\times10^{-11}\\) |\n| **150 km** | **1900 K** | **19.3** | **3.4 kPa** | **\\(1.9\\times10^{-10}\\)** |\n| 300 km | 1970 K | 19.9 | 3.9 kPa | \\(1.7\\times10^{-10}\\) |\n| 730 km | 2170 K | 21.2 | 5.2 kPa | \\(1.1\\times10^{-10}\\) |\n| 1500 km | 2520 K | 22.8 | 7.0 kPa | \\(6.6\\times10^{-11}\\) |\n| 2500 km | 2980 K | 22.9 | 9.1 kPa | \\(8.4\\times10^{-11}\\) |\n| **CMB** | **3800 K** | **21.6** | **9.8 kPa** | **\\(2.0\\times10^{-10}\\)** |\n\nThose absolute amplitudes can move by factors of a few with \\(h_2,\\alpha,\\eta\\), etc. The locations are much harder to move.\n\nAnd when I weight by shell volume,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dP}{dr}=4\\pi r^2\\dot e,\n\\]\n\nthe winner is unambiguously the **upper mantle**, around that \\(\\sim150\\)-km depth. Across all the hot-CMB, \\(\\eta_0\\), and \\(\\alpha=0.2\\)–0.3 cases I tried, the shell-integrated maximum stayed there.\n\nIndependent gravity/topography inversion work has since inferred a Venusian low-viscosity zone beginning around \\(80\\) km depth and extending roughly \\(150\\)–\\(300\\) km, with viscosity \\(5\\)–\\(15\\times\\) lower than the mantle below it. Adding that independently inferred LVZ makes the shallow dissipation maximum stronger, not weaker. citeturn484749search0\n\nNow — only after calculating that — put \\(r_*\\) back in.\n\nFor Venus,\n\n\\[\nr_*=a\\left(\\frac{T_s}{T_o}\\right)^2.\n\\]\n\nThe crossings are:\n\n| Blind standard feature | Radius | \\(T_s\\) when \\(r_*\\) reaches it |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| CMB, reference model | 3110 km | **28.91 h** |\n| plausible CMB range | 3038–3425 km | **28.57–30.34 h** |\n| 730-km boundary | 5322 km | **37.82 h** |\n| bottom of inferred LVZ, 315 km | 5737 km | **39.27 h** |\n| standard dissipation maximum, 150 km | 5902 km | **39.827 h** |\n| top of inferred LVZ, 80 km | 5972 km | **40.063 h** |\n| surface | 6052 km | **40.330 h** |\n\nSo the crossover does something geometrically rather striking during despinning:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{enters the silicate mantle at the basal dissipation maximum}\n}\n\\]\n\nthen traverses the mantle and\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{passes through the dominant upper-mantle dissipation maximum immediately before exiting the planet.}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe entire independently inferred upper low-viscosity zone corresponds to only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{39.27\\ {\\rm h}<T_s<40.06\\ {\\rm h}}\n\\]\n\n—less than an hour of spin-period evolution.\n\nAnd the shell maximum itself is at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{T_s\\simeq39.83\\ {\\rm h}},\n\\]\n\nonly about half an hour of day-length evolution before the \\(r_*=R\\) surface crossing.\n\nThat is the eyebrow part.\n\nBut here is the equally important negative result: **ordinary tidal physics does not notice the crossing.**\n\nI evaluated the standard Andrade heating while \\(r_*\\) passes through that LVZ. There is no resonance, spike, or localization when\n\n\\[\nr_*=r_{\\rm diss,max}.\n\\]\n\nThe local tidal heating at 150 km changes smoothly:\n\n\\[\nT_s=39.27{\\rm h}:\\quad \\dot e\\approx3.89\\times10^{-10},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nT_s=39.83{\\rm h}:\\quad \\dot e\\approx3.85\\times10^{-10},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nT_s=40.06{\\rm h}:\\quad \\dot e\\approx3.83\\times10^{-10}\\ {\\rm W\\,m^{-3}}.\n\\]\n\nThat's barely a few-percent change.\n\nSo:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{standard solar tidal dissipation has a maximum there,}\n}\n\\]\n\nbut\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{standard solar tidal dissipation does not become larger because }r_*\\text{ is there.}\n}\n\\]\n\nThat answers our localization question rather sharply. The localization is **not already contained in the ordinary Andrade tide**.\n\nThe energy accounting reinforces that.\n\nAt roughly 40-hour rotation, a reasonable normalization gives total solid-tide heating of order\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\sim0.07-0.34\\ {\\rm TW}},\n\\]\n\ndepending on the allowed Venus tidal lag/rheology.\n\nVenus's radiogenic mantle heating alone in the Armann–Tackley model is around\n\n\\[\n(3.3\\times10^{24}{\\rm kg})\n(5.2\\times10^{-12}{\\rm W/kg})\n\\sim\n\\boxed{17\\ {\\rm TW}}.\n\\]\n\nSo the ordinary solar tide is roughly \\(0.5\\)–\\(2\\%\\) of that heat source. citeturn149473view3\n\nIt cannot directly melt the LVZ. Even letting the solid tide alone carry Venus through the \\(80\\)–\\(315\\) km crossover interval gives about \\(0.47\\) Gyr in my nominal Andrade spin-down calculation, but only a few\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{{\\rm kJ/kg}}\n\\]\n\nof extra tidal energy locally.\n\nSilicate heat-plus-melt requirements are of order\n\n\\[\n\\sim10^3\\ {\\rm kJ/kg},\n\\]\n\ndepending strongly on starting temperature, pressure and melt fraction.\n\nAnd over \\(0.47\\) Gyr, thermal diffusion with\n\n\\[\n\\kappa\\sim10^{-6}\\ {\\rm m^2/s}\n\\]\n\ncovers roughly\n\n\\[\n\\sqrt{\\kappa t}\\sim120\\ {\\rm km}.\n\\]\n\nSo ordinary tidal heating isn't only weak; on that slow clock it isn't wonderfully localized thermally either.\n\nBut the **rotational reservoir** is a different story.\n\nBetween crossover entry into the mantle at \\(T_s\\simeq28.91\\) h and exit through the surface at \\(40.33\\) h,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta E_{\\rm rot}\n=\n\\frac12 C(\\Omega_{29}^2-\\Omega_{40}^2)\n\\]\n\nis approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{5.2\\times10^{28}\\ {\\rm J}}.\n\\]\n\nThat's huge.\n\nThe standard Andrade model doesn't concentrate it at \\(r_*\\). But Armann & Tackley's Venus overturn calculations use lithospheric yield stresses around \\(100\\) MPa, with episodic global overturn when yielding occurs. citeturn921724search1\n\nThat tells me exactly where to go next.\n\nThe serious “wrung Venus” calculation is not another tidal-heating calculation. Their plastic law uses Byerlee friction \\(0.5\\) capped at \\(100\\) MPa; importantly, their \\(100\\)-MPa cases produce episodic global overturns, while substantially lower yield strengths tend toward continuous mobility and higher ones toward local/stagnant behavior. citeturn455878view0turn455878view2turn455878view4\n\nFor Venus's secular rotational deformation, the measured moment-of-inertia factor,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{C}{MR^2}\\simeq0.337,\n\\]\n\ngives a fluid degree-2 displacement Love number of roughly\n\n\\[\nh_2^f\\simeq1.98\n\\]\n\nunder the standard Radau-Darwin approximation. The MoI itself is uncertain, but \\(0.337\\) is the current central estimate. citeturn677344search3\n\nThen the equilibrium degree-2 rotational strain scale is\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon_2(r,\\Omega)\n\\simeq\n\\frac{h_2^f\\Omega^2r}{3g}.\n\\]\n\nBetween a 29-hour Venus and the blind \\(r_*=R\\) crossing at \\(40.33\\) h, the surface value changes from\n\n\\[\n1.629\\times10^{-3}\n\\]\n\nto\n\n\\[\n8.423\\times10^{-4}.\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta\\epsilon_2\\simeq7.87\\times10^{-4}}.\n\\]\n\nIn displacement language, Venus's equilibrium degree-2 figure changes by about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta \\xi_2\\simeq4.76\\ {\\rm km}}.\n\\]\n\nThat's not tiny.\n\nNow let the material respond through the ordinary Maxwell equation,\n\n\\[\n\\dot\\sigma+\\frac{\\sigma}{\\tau_M}\n=\n2\\mu\\dot\\epsilon_2,\n\\qquad\n\\tau_M=\\frac{\\eta(T,P)}{\\mu},\n\\]\n\nwith plastic failure when the stress hits the Byerlee/yield envelope.\n\nThe blind result is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\sigma_{\\max}\\simeq95\\ {\\rm MPa}}\n\\]\n\nin the cold upper several kilometres of the lithosphere.\n\nThat barely depends on whether I let the 29→40.33 h evolution take \\(0.64\\) Gyr or \\(2.68\\) Gyr, because the coldest lid retains the deformation elastically. Those two clocks correspond roughly to standard solid-tide \\(Q=12\\) and \\(Q=50\\) normalizations; actual Venus spin evolution is more complicated because atmospheric thermal tides and core coupling matter. citeturn521305search2turn521305search6turn521305search0\n\nAt depth, however, relaxation matters enormously. Representative maximum secular despinning stresses are roughly\n\n\\[\n\\begin{array}{c|c}\n\\text{depth} & \\sigma_{\\rm despin}\\\\\n\\hline\n8\\ {\\rm km} & 94\\!-\\!95\\ {\\rm MPa}\\\\\n30\\ {\\rm km} & 14\\!-\\!48\\ {\\rm MPa}\\\\\n50\\ {\\rm km} & \\sim1\\ {\\rm MPa}\\\\\n80\\ {\\rm km} & \\sim7\\times10^{-3}\\ {\\rm MPa}\\\\\n150\\ {\\rm km} & \\text{a few Pa}\n\\end{array}\n\\]\n\ndepending mainly on the spin-evolution clock.\n\nSo the deep warm mantle simply oozes into the changing equilibrium figure. The cold lid does not.\n\nAnd now we have a genuinely interesting standard-physics coincidence:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{blind despinning stress}\\sim95\\ {\\rm MPa}}\n\\]\n\nversus the independently chosen Venus episodic-overturn model value\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\sigma_y\\sim100\\ {\\rm MPa}}.\n\\]\n\nThat does **not** mean despinning caused Venus's resurfacing. The stress estimate has order-unity model uncertainties. But it says changing Venus from the 29-hour to 40-hour figure naturally puts the cold lithosphere in precisely the mechanical regime where existing Venus convection calculations change tectonic mode. Armann & Tackley's \\(100\\)-MPa runs generate 5–8 global overturns, each typically lasting about \\(150\\) Myr. citeturn677344search0turn455878view4\n\nThe heating result is equally important—and negative.\n\nThe maximum accumulated dissipation from this secular figure adjustment is only about\n\n\\[\n1.5\\times10^4\\ {\\rm J/m^3},\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\n\\sim4\\ {\\rm J/kg}.\n\\]\n\nWith \\(c_p=1200\\ {\\rm J\\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta T_{\\rm despin}\\sim0.004\\ {\\rm K}}.\n\\]\n\nCompare that with the published latent heat alone,\n\n\\[\nL\\simeq600\\,000\\ {\\rm J/kg}.\n\\]\n\nSo:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{despinning stress can be important; despinning heat cannot melt Venus.}}\n\\]\n\nThat changes the prospective mechanism substantially. The changing rotational figure is potentially a **failure trigger**, not the furnace. The thermal energy has to be the mantle/core's existing thermal budget, radiogenic heat, gravitational potential released by overturn, decompression melting, etc.\n\nWhich is actually much more physically interesting.\n\nNow overlay \\(r_*\\).\n\nThe blind crossover reaches the following depths at these Venus rotation periods:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{array}{c|c}\n\\text{depth} & T_s\\text{ when }r_*\\text{ reaches it}\\\\\n\\hline\n{\\rm CMB}\\;(2942\\,{\\rm km}) & 28.91\\ {\\rm h}\\\\\n730\\ {\\rm km} & 37.82\\ {\\rm h}\\\\\n315\\ {\\rm km} & 39.27\\ {\\rm h}\\\\\n150\\ {\\rm km} & 39.83\\ {\\rm h}\\\\\n80\\ {\\rm km} & 40.07\\ {\\rm h}\\\\\n30\\ {\\rm km} & 40.23\\ {\\rm h}\\\\\n\\text{surface} & 40.33\\ {\\rm h}\n\\end{array}\n\\]\n\nAnd here is where it gets peculiar.\n\nIndependent gravity/topography inversion finds a Venusian low-viscosity zone beginning around \\(80\\) km depth and extending roughly \\(235\\) km downward—so approximately \\(80\\)–\\(315\\) km—with viscosity \\(5\\)–\\(15\\times\\) lower than below it and possibly associated with partial melt. citeturn355591search0turn355591search1\n\nSo \\(r_*\\) crosses that entire independently inferred weak/possibly partially molten zone during only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{39.27\\ {\\rm h}\\rightarrow40.07\\ {\\rm h}}.\n\\]\n\nDuring that passage, the accumulated maximum stress in the cold lid rises from about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{89\\ {\\rm MPa}\\rightarrow93\\ {\\rm MPa}}.\n\\]\n\nThen \\(r_*\\) traverses the final \\(\\sim80\\) km while the lid approaches\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{95\\ {\\rm MPa}}.\n\\]\n\nSo the standard-physics picture at the terminal sweep is not:\n\n\\[\n\\text{crossover heats rock until it melts}.\n\\]\n\nIt is much more like\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{array}{c}\n\\text{already-hot, weak / partly molten upper mantle}\\\\\n\\updownarrow\\\\\n\\text{cold strong stagnant lid approaching its yield stress}\\\\\n\\end{array}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhile the SAT crossover passes from the weak layer into the stressed lid.\n\nThat's a considerably better candidate for “twist, melt, ooze.”\n\nAnd now the timescale calculation.\n\nFor a \\(Q=12\\) solid-body despinning clock, the whole 29→40.33 h interval is approximately \\(643\\) Myr. For \\(Q=50\\), about \\(2.68\\) Gyr.\n\nOnce \\(r_*\\) reaches:\n\n\\[\n315\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\nthe remaining time before it exits Venus is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{44\\ {\\rm Myr}\\quad(Q=12)}\n\\]\n\nto\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{185\\ {\\rm Myr}\\quad(Q=50)}.\n\\]\n\nFrom 150 km:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{21-86\\ {\\rm Myr}}.\n\\]\n\nFrom 80 km:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{11-45\\ {\\rm Myr}}.\n\\]\n\nFrom 30 km:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{4-17\\ {\\rm Myr}}.\n\\]\n\nNow we finally uncover the standard geodynamic number:\n\nArmann & Tackley's episodic Venus solutions give typical global overturn durations of about\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{150\\ {\\rm Myr}}.\n\\]\n\nOur completely independent \\(r_*\\) sweep from the bottom of the inferred upper-mantle LVZ to the surface gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{44-185\\ {\\rm Myr}}\n\\]\n\nover the quite ordinary \\(Q=12\\)–50 bracket.\n\nIn fact, \\(Q\\simeq40\\) would give almost exactly \\(150\\) Myr for that particular sweep.\n\nI would absolutely **not** fit \\(Q=40\\) and announce victory. Venus's ancient dissipation and atmospheric torque history are too uncertain for that.\n\nBut this is precisely what a retrodiction candidate looks like:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{array}{c}\n\\text{geometry calculated first}\\\\\nr_*:\\;315{\\rm\\ km}\\rightarrow0\\\\\n\\Downarrow\\\\\n\\text{tens to hundreds of Myr}\\\\\n\\\\\n\\text{independent convection model}\\\\\n\\Downarrow\\\\\n\\sim150{\\rm\\ Myr\\ global\\ overturn}\n\\end{array}}\n\\]\n\nThere is one more physically important insulation result. Pure conduction across the roughly \\(120\\) km between the \\(150\\)-km weak/dissipative region and a \\(30\\)-km mechanical lid takes, for\n\n\\[\n\\kappa\\sim10^{-6}\\ {\\rm m^2/s},\n\\]\n\nabout\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{4.6\\times10^8\\ {\\rm yr}}.\n\\]\n\nThat's longer than much of the terminal crossover interval.\n\nSo a resurfacing cascade cannot simply be “heat conducts upward.” It has to involve mechanical failure, convection, melt segregation, buoyant transport, decompression, intrusive heating, or some combination. Which is exactly what actual planetary melting and resurfacing look like.\n\nMy read of the calculation is therefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\textbf{The first plausible role for }r_*\\textbf{ is not an energy source.             "Yes. The clean mental picture is simpler than all the equations made it look.\n\nVenus is slowing down. As it slows, the shape that a rotating planet “wants” to have changes. A fast-spinning planet wants a larger equatorial bulge; a slower one wants to be rounder.\n\nThe deep, hot mantle can accommodate that change by flowing. It basically oozes toward the new equilibrium shape. The cold outer lid cannot adjust nearly as easily, so it carries stress.\n\nIn our calculation, taking Venus through the particular spin range we care about—roughly a 29-hour day to a 40-hour day—the equilibrium figure changes by an amount corresponding to several kilometres of degree-2 deformation. Most of the warm mantle relaxes that stress away. The cold lithosphere doesn't.\n\nThat leaves the outer lid carrying stresses approaching roughly\n\n\\[\n\\sim 100\\ {\\rm MPa}.\n\\]\n\nAnd that is interesting because standard Venus convection models independently use yield stresses of roughly that magnitude in regimes where the planet changes from relatively stagnant behavior into episodic large-scale/global overturn.\n\nSo the first part of the mental map is:\n\n\\[\n\\text{Venus slows}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{preferred planetary shape changes}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{hot interior flows}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{cold lid gets increasingly stressed}.\n\\]\n\nNow separately, SAT's spin/orbit mapping gives us the crossover cylinder \\(r_*\\). It is not a material shell and it is not something standard physics says is physically present. It's the location in our remapping where the spin-associated and orbital-associated curvature scales are equal.\n\nAs Venus slows, that cylinder expands outward.\n\nAt about a 29-hour day it is around the core-mantle boundary.\n\nThen it sweeps outward through the mantle.\n\nAt around 39.3 hours it reaches roughly 315 km below the surface.\n\nAround 39.8 hours it reaches about 150 km depth.\n\nAround 40.1 hours it reaches about 80 km depth.\n\nAt 40.33 hours it reaches the surface and leaves the planet.\n\nNow here's the striking independent fact: Venus appears to have a weak upper-mantle zone roughly in that \\(80\\)–\\(315\\) km depth range. It may be hotter, lower-viscosity, perhaps partly molten.\n\nSo near the end of the sweep, our geometry is doing this:\n\n\\[\nr_*:\n\\quad\n\\text{deep mantle}\n\\longrightarrow\n\\boxed{\\text{weak upper mantle}}\n\\longrightarrow\n\\boxed{\\text{stressed lithosphere}}\n\\longrightarrow\n\\text{surface}.\n\\]\n\nAt the same time, standard rotational mechanics says the cold lid has accumulated something like \\(90\\)–\\(100\\) MPa of despinning stress.\n\nThat is the coincidence.\n\nWhat we did **not** find is equally important.\n\nThe ordinary tidal heating is far too weak to melt Venus.\n\nThe ordinary elastic energy associated with changing the rotational figure is also far too weak to melt Venus.\n\nSo our calculation does **not** say:\n\n\\[\n\\text{spin-down energy heats mantle}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{Venus melts}.\n\\]\n\nInstead it suggests something more like:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{hot planet already containing enormous thermal energy}\n+\n\\text{weak/possibly partly molten mantle}\n+\n\\text{increasingly stressed cold lid}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{possible mechanical failure/overturn}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIn that picture, the rotational evolution is a trigger or loading mechanism. The furnace is already there.\n\nThink of a pot of very thick hot material with a rigid crust on top. You don't need to supply enough mechanical work to melt the contents. They're already hot and slowly convecting. You need to alter the stresses enough that the lid can no longer maintain its previous configuration.\n\nThen once failure begins, ordinary geology supplies large additional effects: hot material rises, pressure falls, decompression melting increases, melt weakens the rock, buoyancy moves more material upward, lithospheric failure allows more heat transport, and so forth. That's where something can cascade.\n\nAnd this is where “twist, melt, ooze” needs a slight translation from the rope image.\n\nThe “ooze” part is already plainly present in the standard calculation: the hot mantle continually relaxes toward the changing rotational figure.\n\nThe “melt” part is primarily the planet's thermal/rheological state, not heat generated directly by the despinning.\n\nThe “twist” part is the one we haven't yet demonstrated literally. What we have established in standard mechanics is changing rotational figure and differential relaxation. Whether the full \\(3+3\\) worldtube description reveals that as an actual accumulated winding/shear structure is still the SAT question.\n\nAnd \\(r_*\\) currently has a very specific epistemic status:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{It is an independently calculated geometric marker that passes through a very interesting part of the thermomechanical system.}}\n\\]\n\nWe have **not yet shown that matter cares about \\(r_*\\)**.\n\nThat's the key distinction.\n\nWhat makes the result worth pursuing is that we calculated \\(r_*\\) from spin and orbit, independently calculated the standard stress/rheology, and only afterward discovered that the terminal \\(r_*\\) sweep crosses the weak upper mantle just as the cold lid approaches a standard-model failure regime.\n\nAnd the clocks aren't absurdly different either. Depending on the spin-evolution model, the sweep from the bottom of that weak upper zone to the surface is on the order of tens to a couple hundred million years. Standard episodic Venus-overturn models can produce events lasting around \\(10^8\\) years.\n\nSo the plain-English candidate is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Venus gradually winds down; its interior oozes into the new shape, its lid cannot keep up, and eventually the hot weak interior may reorganize beneath a lid that is near failure.}\n}\n\\]\n\nSAT then notices that its independently defined geometric crossover happens to sweep through the weak zone during that terminal episode.\n\nThat's what we've actually got. The next leap—“the crossover helps *cause* or organize the failure”—is exactly what remains to be demonstrated rather than assumed."

            "Exactly. The issue is not “avoid assumptions.” It is “make the assumption explicit, bounded, and testable.”\n\nFor this Venus problem, we should actively branch the model.\n\nOne branch says the crossover radius is merely descriptive geometry and matter does not respond to it in any special way. Then standard despinning, mantle convection, tidal forcing, plastic yielding, and thermal evolution proceed exactly as usual, and r-star is just a useful map overlay.\n\nAnother branch says the crossover marks a change in how rotational and orbital worldtube curvature are resolved mechanically. Then we should calculate what follows if stress transfer, dissipation, or rheological weakening is enhanced in some neighborhood of r-star.\n\nA stronger branch says the planet really behaves like a wrung, partially relaxing worldtube bundle, so the crossover is part of a moving torsional/shear structure. Then we derive the consequences of that assumption and see whether they resemble known things like episodic overturn, resurfacing, magnetic reversals, mantle plume organization, or spin evolution.\n\nAnd there can be deliberately extreme branches too. For example: assume perfect localization at r-star; assume zero localization; assume localization width set by a Maxwell length; assume the crossover only matters in fluids; assume it only matters where the material is already near yield. Those are useful because they give upper and lower bounds.\n\nThe important thing is to keep the logic conditional:\n\nIf assumption A is true, then consequence X follows.\n\nIf assumption A is false, X should disappear.\n\nIf two very different assumptions produce the same observable, that observable is not discriminating.\n\nIf one branch predicts something unique and measurable, that becomes a real test.\n\nSo yes, assumptions are part of the machinery. They are how we map the possible solution space. The mistake would be letting a useful exploratory assumption quietly harden into a claimed property of SAT before the comparison has been done."

            "Then I’d push Venus through a deliberately wide assumption fan and see which branches die fastest.\n\nThe clean baseline is already fixed: standard despinning changes the equilibrium figure by kilometres; the hot mantle relaxes; the cold lid can accumulate stresses approaching roughly \\(10^2\\) MPa; ordinary tidal heating is too weak to melt the planet; and the blind crossover \\(r_*\\) sweeps from the deep mantle through the independently inferred weak upper mantle and then the lithosphere as the day length approaches about 40 hours.\n\nNow take four aggressive branches.\n\n1. **\\(r_*\\) is dynamically irrelevant.**  \nThen it is just a coordinate marker. Venus resurfacing must come entirely from ordinary stagnant-lid convection, episodic overturn, plume activity, phase transitions, atmosphere–solid torque evolution, etc. The fact that \\(r_*\\) traverses the weak zone near the mechanical-failure regime is coincidence. This is our null model.\n\n2. **\\(r_*\\) localizes stress transfer, but not heat directly.**  \nThen the changing worldtube geometry concentrates differential stress or strain-rate near a moving band. The important consequence is not melting by friction; it is earlier yielding. A region already thermally weak gets mechanically selected, fails, rises, decompresses, melts more, and unloads the lid. This is presently the most physically economical “wrung Venus” branch.\n\n3. **\\(r_*\\) localizes dissipation.**  \nHere we explicitly allow some fraction \\(f\\) of the ordinary rotational-energy loss to be deposited in a band of thickness \\(\\delta\\) around the crossover. We can then calculate the threshold \\(f(\\delta)\\) needed to heat that material to solidus or partial melt. If it demands \\(f>1\\), dead. If it needs \\(10^{-6}\\), suspiciously easy. If it needs a few percent, potentially interesting.\n\n4. **\\(r_*\\) marks a true torsional state change of the worldtube bundle.**  \nThis is the strongest SAT branch. The planet is not fundamentally a succession of spinning spheres but a continually wound extended object; solids retain some winding elastically, liquids redistribute it, gases advect it. When the relative spin/orbit geometry reaches a critical configuration, the preferred mode of distributing that winding changes. Then resurfacing, magnetic reversals, atmospheric circulation changes and perhaps orbital evolution are different readouts of the same higher-order transition. This one should make additional predictions or die.\n\nThe quickest useful calculation is branch 3, because we can bound it brutally.\n\nTake an active band around the Venus crossover of radial thickness \\(\\delta\\). Near the upper mantle, its mass is approximately\n\n\\[\nM_{\\rm band}\\sim 4\\pi R^2\\rho\\,\\delta\n\\]\n\nto order of magnitude. With \\(R\\approx6.05\\times10^6\\) m and \\(\\rho\\approx3300\\ {\\rm kg\\,m^{-3}}\\),\n\na 10-km band contains roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1.5\\times10^{22}\\ {\\rm kg}},\n\\]\n\na 100-km band roughly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1.5\\times10^{23}\\ {\\rm kg}}.\n\\]\n\nIf the heat-plus-partial-melt requirement is of order\n\n\\[\nq\\sim10^6\\ {\\rm J/kg},\n\\]\n\nthen the required energies are approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1.5\\times10^{28}\\ {\\rm J}}\n\\]\n\nfor 10 km and\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1.5\\times10^{29}\\ {\\rm J}}\n\\]\n\nfor 100 km.\n\nOur ordinary rotational-energy loss over the interesting \\(29\\rightarrow40\\) hour interval was of order\n\n\\[\n\\Delta E_{\\rm rot}\\sim5\\times10^{28}\\ {\\rm J}.\n\\]\n\nSo perfect localization tells us immediately:\n\nA 10-km globally continuous band could in principle be driven deeply into melting with a substantial fraction of the available rotational reservoir.\n\nA 100-km globally continuous band cannot be wholesale melted from that reservoir alone; it would require several times the total available despinning energy.\n\nThat is already a useful boundary.\n\nMore precisely, the required localization fraction is roughly\n\n\\[\nf_{\\rm req}\n\\sim\n\\frac{M_{\\rm band}q}{\\Delta E_{\\rm rot}}.\n\\]\n\nSo approximately:\n\n\\[\n\\delta=1\\ {\\rm km}\n\\Rightarrow\nf_{\\rm req}\\sim0.03,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\delta=10\\ {\\rm km}\n\\Rightarrow\nf_{\\rm req}\\sim0.3,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\delta=30\\ {\\rm km}\n\\Rightarrow\nf_{\\rm req}\\sim0.9,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\delta=100\\ {\\rm km}\n\\Rightarrow\nf_{\\rm req}\\sim3.\n\\]\n\nThat means if direct despinning energy is doing the melting, the active mechanically selected band must be fairly narrow—tens of kilometres at most—or the planet's pre-existing thermal energy must supply most of the enthalpy.\n\nAnd the latter is actually more plausible. If the mantle is already only, say, 100–300 K below local solidus, then the required *extra* energy is much smaller than \\(1\\) MJ/kg. A 100 K deficit plus latent heat might be around \\(0.7\\) MJ/kg; if only a modest melt fraction is needed to collapse viscosity, the effective threshold could be far below full-melt enthalpy.\n\nSo branch 2 becomes more attractive than branch 3:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{mechanical localization triggers failure; existing planetary heat does most of the melting.}}\n\\]\n\nNow the adventurous next step is obvious. We should calculate the critical band thickness and localization fraction across a matrix of assumptions:\n\n\\[\n\\delta=1,10,30,100,300\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\npartial-melt targets of perhaps\n\n\\[\n1\\%,\\ 5\\%,\\ 20\\%,\\ 100\\%,\n\\]\n\nand starting temperatures 50, 100, 300 and 500 K below solidus.\n\nThat will tell us which combinations are impossible, which are trivial, and which occupy the interesting middle territory.\n\nThen we can do the same exercise for Earth. If the same geometry predicts that Earth is nowhere near a Venus-style runaway but does naturally support smaller localized mantle events, *then* the Deccan/Yellowstone thought becomes worth sharpening. If it predicts Venus-scale failure for Earth too, something in the branch is wrong.\n\nThat is where I’d go next."

            "Yes. That is the correction. “Not enough heating” is not a meaningful statement without a heat-loss model and a duration. The relevant quantity is the integrated net enthalpy budget.\n\nFor a mantle volume, schematically,\n\n\\[\n\\rho c_p\\frac{dT}{dt}\n=\nq_{\\rm tide}\n+q_{\\rm other}\n-q_{\\rm loss}\n-\\rho L\\frac{df_m}{dt}.\n\\]\n\nIf the net term on the right stays positive, even weak tidal heating accumulates. With perfect insulation, any nonzero persistent heating eventually raises the temperature to the solidus. Once melting begins, latent heat slows the temperature rise while melt fraction grows. So the question is exactly as you put it:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{Does our mechanism materially change when the system reaches the tipping point?}}\n\\]\n\nAnd a second question:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{Does it impose a distinctive cyclic or secular signature on that approach?}}\n\\]\n\nThere is a useful calculation we can already make.\n\nFor silicate thermal diffusivity around\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_T\\sim10^{-6}\\ {\\rm m^2/s},\n\\]\n\nthe conductive relaxation time over thickness \\(L\\) is roughly\n\n\\[\n\\tau_{\\rm diff}\\sim\\frac{L^2}{\\kappa_T}.\n\\]\n\nThat gives approximately:\n\n\\[\n10\\ {\\rm km}\\rightarrow3.2\\ {\\rm Myr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n50\\ {\\rm km}\\rightarrow79\\ {\\rm Myr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n100\\ {\\rm km}\\rightarrow317\\ {\\rm Myr},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n200\\ {\\rm km}\\rightarrow1.27\\ {\\rm Gyr}.\n\\]\n\nNow compare those with the blind Venus \\(r_*\\) sweep times we got.\n\nThe crossover moving from roughly 315 km depth to the surface took, depending on the ordinary despinning normalization,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\sim44-185\\ {\\rm Myr}.}\n\\]\n\nThat's suddenly quite interesting.\n\nA 50-km thermal structure has a conductive relaxation time of order\n\n\\[\n80\\ {\\rm Myr},\n\\]\n\nright inside that interval.\n\nA 100-km structure retains heat for longer than the entire terminal sweep.\n\nSo the relevant regime is not\n\n\\[\n\\text{heating event}\\ll\\text{thermal time}\n\\]\n\nnor necessarily\n\n\\[\n\\text{heating event}\\gg\\text{thermal time}.\n\\]\n\nWe are plausibly near\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\tau_{\\rm forcing}\\sim\\tau_{\\rm thermal}}\n\\]\n\nfor tens-of-kilometres-scale lithosphere/upper-mantle structure.\n\nThat is exactly where a modest change in forcing or heat transport can move the timing of a threshold dramatically.\n\nSuppose without the SAT-associated localization/remapping effect a volume has net heating\n\n\\[\nq_0=q_{\\rm in}-q_{\\rm loss}>0.\n\\]\n\nIf its enthalpy deficit to some rheological transition is \\(\\Delta h\\), the crude tipping time is\n\n\\[\nt_0\\simeq\\frac{\\rho\\Delta h}{q_0}.\n\\]\n\nNow assume our mechanism changes the effective heating or insulation by fractional amount \\(\\delta\\):\n\n\\[\nq_1=q_0+\\delta q.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nt_1=\\frac{\\rho\\Delta h}{q_0+\\delta q}.\n\\]\n\nThe interesting behavior occurs when the system is already close to thermal balance:\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm in}\\approx q_{\\rm loss}.\n\\]\n\nIf, say,\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm in}=1.05q_{\\rm loss},\n\\]\n\nthe net accumulation is only\n\n\\[\n0.05q_{\\rm loss}.\n\\]\n\nAn extra heating/localization contribution of merely\n\n\\[\n0.05q_{\\rm loss}\n\\]\n\nthen doubles the net accumulation rate and halves the tipping time.\n\nIf\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm in}=1.01q_{\\rm loss},\n\\]\n\na one-percent perturbation comparable to the heat-loss rate can change the accumulated heating rate by order unity.\n\nSo there is a crucial distinction:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{small fraction of total heat flow}\\neq\\text{small effect on tipping time}.}\n\\]\n\nNear a thermal-rheological threshold, what matters is the perturbation relative to the small difference\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm in}-q_{\\rm out},\n\\]\n\nnot relative to either large term individually.\n\nThat may rescue the significance of ordinary tidal heating rather dramatically. We previously compared tidal power to radiogenic heat and found it smaller. But if convection/conduction removes nearly all the background heat, then a comparatively small persistent tidal contribution can dominate the **net secular accumulation**.\n\nInsulation makes this even more nonlinear. Once viscosity falls, convection can either increase heat removal and stabilize the system or reorganize into localized melt transport and destabilize the lid. Melt changes viscosity, thermal conductivity, buoyancy and latent-heat storage simultaneously.\n\nSo the tipping calculation ultimately wants something like\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^{t_*}\n\\left[\nq_{\\rm tide}\n+q_{\\rm secular}\n+q_{\\rm core}\n-q_{\\rm conductive}\n-q_{\\rm convective}\n\\right]dt\n=\n\\rho\\left(c_p\\Delta T+Lf_m\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nOur mechanism matters if it significantly changes either side's trajectory before \\(t_*\\).\n\nNow the cyclic signature.\n\nThe fast astronomical forcing gets filtered very strongly by the mantle. For periodic thermal forcing of angular frequency \\(\\omega\\), the conductive skin depth is\n\n\\[\n\\delta_T=\\sqrt{\\frac{2\\kappa_T}{\\omega}}\n=\n\\sqrt{\\frac{\\kappa_T P}{\\pi}}.\n\\]\n\nFor a Venus-year-scale period of about 225 days,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\delta_T\\sim2.5\\ {\\rm m}.}\n\\]\n\nSo the deep mantle cannot thermally follow the orbital cycle. It sees its time-averaged dissipation.\n\nThat's helpful: we should **not** expect deep melting to oscillate every Venus year.\n\nAt longer periods:\n\n\\[\n100\\ {\\rm kyr}\\rightarrow\n\\delta_T\\sim1\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n1\\ {\\rm Myr}\\rightarrow\n\\sim3\\ {\\rm km},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n100\\ {\\rm Myr}\\rightarrow\n\\sim32\\ {\\rm km}.\n\\]\n\nSo deep thermal behavior naturally acts as a huge low-pass filter.\n\nBut mechanical stress doesn't have to wait for thermal diffusion. Orbital, rotational and tidal stresses can be cyclic immediately; their **dissipation** is rectified into positive heat:\n\n\\[\n+\\tau\\dot\\epsilon\n\\]\n\naveraged over each cycle.\n\nThat gives us a potentially distinctive hierarchy:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{fast astronomical cycle}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{cyclic mechanical strain}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{positive mean dissipation}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{slow thermal accumulation}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{threshold}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{rapid rheological/geological response}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSo resurfacing need not occur on the forcing period at all.\n\nA system could be loaded cyclically for hundreds of millions of cycles and then fail once.\n\nMore interestingly, if some *slow* astronomical envelope modulates the mean dissipation—for example eccentricity, obliquity, spin evolution, resonance passage, or the \\(r_*\\) migration—then the tipping probability should be phase-biased toward maxima of that envelope.\n\nThat is where we can get an actual cyclic fingerprint.\n\nUnder the current Venus construction, I see at least three clocks that should remain separate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P_{\\rm orbit/spin}}\n\\]\n\nproduces the fast cyclic mechanical forcing;\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\tau_{\\rm thermal}}\n\\]\n\nsets how quickly the dissipated energy can accumulate or escape;\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\tau_{r_*}}\n\\]\n\nsets the secular migration of the geometric crossover through regions of different rheology.\n\nIf the mechanism is real, resurfacing should occur when those three cooperate—not when any one clock “equals the resurfacing period.”\n\nAnd that suggests something stronger to calculate next.\n\nRather than asking whether \\(r_*\\) causes heating, we can calculate a **tipping-time ratio**:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R\n=\n\\frac{t_{\\rm tip,\\;ordinary}}\n{t_{\\rm tip,\\;with\\ crossover\\ coupling}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen sweep crossover coupling from zero to extreme values and thermal insulation from highly conductive to highly insulated.\n\nThat gives us a genuine assumption map:\n\n- when does \\(r_*\\) change tipping time by \\(<1\\%\\)?\n- when does it halve it?\n- when does it move a system from never melting to melting?\n- when does it produce episodic rather than continuous failure?\n- what periodic/secular signature accompanies each regime?\n\nThat is the calculation that will tell us whether the crossover is merely geometrically cute or capable of materially controlling planetary history."

This is exactly the point where we should ask whether we have merely manufactured an evocative ratio.\n\nAnd I don't think the answer is simply “numerology,” although parts of what we've found could still turn out to be coincidences.\n\nThe distinction is this:\n\nIf we had noticed that some melting depth happened to correspond to some arbitrary ratio of spin period to orbital period, that would be nearly worthless. As you say, every pair of numbers has a ratio.\n\nBut that isn't quite what happened.\n\nWe started from the same geometrical operation for every planet:\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_{\\rm spin}(r_\\perp)\n=\n\\kappa_{\\rm orbit},\n\\]\n\nwhich gives\n\n\\[\nr_*\n=\na\\left(\\frac{T_s}{T_o}\\right)^2.\n\\]\n\nThere aren't free planetary coefficients in that equation. We don't choose a different relationship for Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.\n\nThat one construction produces qualitatively different geometrical regimes:\n\nVenus presently has \\(r_*\\) enormously outside the planet.\n\nEarth and Mars have \\(r_*\\) inside substantial liquid interiors.\n\nJupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune have \\(r_*\\) crushed into a tiny axial region and are spin-dominated essentially throughout their bulk.\n\nThat's already stronger than “these periods have ratios,” because the ratio produces a geometrically meaningful location, and that location moves predictably through the body.\n\nThen independent information enters.\n\nFor Earth, the calculated cylinder lands close to the independently known inner-core tangent cylinder.\n\nFor Mars, the same calculation puts the crossover inside the liquid metallic core but not near an inner-core boundary—which is appropriate because Mars apparently lacks Earth's large solid inner-core arrangement.\n\nFor the giant planets, the same calculation says there should effectively be no Earth-like bulk spin/orbit crossover at all.\n\nFor Venus, the same calculation says that if it underwent substantial despinning, \\(r_*\\) must have swept all the way through the planet, with the particularly rapid terminal traversal occurring as its day passed through roughly 29–40 hours.\n\nThen, without using \\(r_*\\) to construct the rheology, we find that Venus has a weak upper-mantle region in the final part of that sweep and that ordinary despinning mechanics can put its cold lid into roughly the stress regime where conventional Venus models transition toward episodic overturn.\n\nThat sequence matters.\n\nIt's not\n\n\\[\n\\text{observe geology}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{choose ratio that reproduces geology}.\n\\]\n\nIt's more like\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{one geometric rule}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{different planetary geometries}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{compare against independently different interiors}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat's the beginning of a relationship.\n\nBut I think SAT is making an even stronger claim than that.\n\nThe interesting object isn't really the number \\(r_*\\). It's the mapping between dynamical scales and material organization.\n\nSomething like:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{spin/orbit history}\n+\n\\text{planetary size}\n+\n\\text{internal state}\n\\longrightarrow\n\\text{where competing geometrical contributions are resolved inside the body}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen solid, liquid and gas systems respond differently to the same mapped geometry.\n\nThat is much closer to what we'd need for SAT to have explanatory content.\n\nConsider the cross-planet comparison in that form.\n\nEarth has a large fluid core straddling the crossover and a solid inner core sitting rather close to its cylinder. We see vigorous core dynamics and magnetic polarity reversals, while the whole planet obviously doesn't execute Dzhanibekov flips.\n\nMars has similar normalized crossover geometry but a very different thermal history and interior structure. Its global dynamo died; the old crust records a once-active dynamo. So crossover geometry alone clearly isn't sufficient.\n\nThat's good. A simplistic theory already fails.\n\nVenus has no internal crossover today. If its spin history swept that crossover outward through the planet, its thermomechanical history should be radically different from Earth's. Independently, Venus is the terrestrial planet most strongly associated with extensive or perhaps near-global resurfacing.\n\nThe giants are essentially everywhere on the opposite side of the crossover. If we tried to explain their observable dynamics using an Earth-style crossover mechanism, we'd immediately fail. Instead they should express rotational organization mostly through fluid differential rotation, vorticity, jets and magnetic-fluid dynamics—which is at least qualitatively the regime they occupy.\n\nThat is the kind of cross-system correspondence we need.\n\nThere is also a very important falsification criterion.\n\nSuppose we calculate \\(r_*\\) for a large sample of planets and exoplanets and discover that interior phase boundaries, dynamical transitions, magnetic behavior, resurfacing histories, etc. bear no systematic relationship whatsoever to the geometrical class.\n\nThen \\(r_*\\) was a pretty coincidence.\n\nEspecially the Earth tangent cylinder.\n\nOne 9-percent match isn't enough.\n\nWhat would make it increasingly difficult to dismiss is if the same construction repeatedly predicts things of the form:\n\n\\[\nr_* \\text{ inside liquid conductor}\n\\rightarrow A,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nr_* \\text{ near solid/liquid boundary}\n\\rightarrow B,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nr_* \\text{ outside body}\n\\rightarrow C,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nr_*/R\\ll1\n\\rightarrow D,\n\\]\n\nwith \\(A,B,C,D\\) specified **before** looking at the next objects.\n\nThen we're no longer discussing a ratio. We're discussing an empirical mapping.\n\nAnd SAT has another advantage here: \\(r_*\\) isn't an arbitrary dimensionless number. It corresponds to equality of two actual geometric invariants in the representation:\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_s=\\kappa_o.\n\\]\n\nSo there is a structural reason for the boundary to exist.\n\nThe question we haven't answered is whether that equality has material dynamical significance. Standard mechanics doesn't automatically say it does.\n\nBut SAT's stronger proposition could be precisely:\n\n> The equality is significant because spin and orbital motion are not independent motions pasted onto a three-dimensional ball; they are components of one extended worldtube geometry, and matter must continuously accommodate their combined geometry.\n\nIf that's right, then \\(r_*\\) is not “the radius where two interesting numbers happen to be equal.” It is the locus where the relative dominance of two contributions to the same extended history reverses:\n\n\\[\n\\chi<1\n\\quad\\longleftrightarrow\\quad\n\\chi>1.\n\\]\n\nAnd that gives us something stronger still: **the gradient matters**.\n\nOn one side,\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_o>\\kappa_s;\n\\]\n\non the other,\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_s>\\kappa_o.\n\\]\n\nA material body crossing that surface is therefore moving between two geometrical regimes. If the worldtube has any finite capacity for transmitting shear, twist, vorticity, stress or phase information, we'd expect something to happen in the transition region.\n\nWhat happens depends upon material state.\n\nThat's very different from saying “melting occurs at period ratio \\(x\\).”\n\nIt's saying:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{one geometrical transition is being expressed through different constitutive physics in different planets.}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd that's testable.\n\nI think the most important comparison we've accidentally created is actually **Earth versus Mars versus Venus**.\n\nEarth and Mars give us two internal-crossover terrestrial planets with different phase architecture.\n\nVenus gives us a terrestrial planet whose crossover plausibly migrated completely through its interior.\n\nMercury gives us another orbit-dominated rocky control without Venus's extraordinary size, atmosphere and thermal state.\n\nIf the worldtube mapping is meaningful, those four ought to form a coherent sequence—not four unrelated anecdotes.\n\nThat's what I would calculate next: construct the terrestrial-planet phase diagram using only external quantities first—\\(M,R,a,T_s,T_o,\\epsilon,e\\)—map \\(r_*(t)\\) or its possible history, and only afterward lay the independently inferred core/mantle/phase structures and geological histories over it.\n\nIf a coherent pattern survives that exercise, we're beginning to get beyond numerology. If we have to keep inventing a different story for every planet, we're not."
